repository.readme:
**Test your RAG components against a real stack, not a toy baseline. Then give that stack to your agent.** Code for **[Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)**
[Ido Levy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/idolevi31/)1,2 · [Segev Shlomov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/segev-shlomov/)1 · [Leshem Choshen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leshemchoshen/)1,2
1IBM · 2Weizmann Institute of Science [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.29722-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722) [![Project page](https://img.shields.io/badge/project-page-1f6feb.svg)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-read-1f6feb.svg)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/docs/) [![Podcast](https://img.shields.io/badge/podcast-25_min-1f6feb.svg?logo=data%3Aimage%2Fsvg%2Bxml%3Bbase64%%3D%3D)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#podcast) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/lasagna-rag.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/lasagna-rag/) [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/1428808706.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23548068) [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/LICENSE) [![Python 3.10 to 3.13](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%20|%203.11%20|%203.12%20|%203.13-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![Tests](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/actions/workflows/tests.yml) [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/notebooks/compare_your_reranker.ipynb) **[Quickstart](#quickstart)** · **[Compare a component](#compare-a-component)** · **[Give your agent RAG](#give-your-agent-rag-mcp-rest-docker)** · **[Docs](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/docs/)** · **[The paper](#the-paper)**


A real run with the idle waits cut: write a reranker, sweep it against a built-in, and get a Holm-corrected verdict.

| You want to | Start here | |---|---| | Show that your component helps, with a significance test and no API key | [Compare a component](#compare-a-component) | | Give an agent search over your own documents (MCP, REST, Docker) | [Give your agent RAG](#give-your-agent-rag-mcp-rest-docker) | | Pick a vector backend and retrieval strategy without building a harness | [Quickstart](#quickstart), then [What's inside](#whats-inside) | | Read what the paper found | [The paper](#the-paper) | --- ## The problem Most RAG results are reported one component at a time. A new reranker is measured against a baseline with no query augmentation, no agentic loop, and an old chunker, because building the rest of the stack just to run the comparison is more work than the contribution itself. That makes published gains hard to add up. If a reranker claims +4 NDCG and a query expander claims +3, you cannot tell from the papers whether stacking them gives you **+7, +4, or -1**. Lasagna exists to make that question answerable. ``` ┌─────────── your component drops in here ───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → rerank → augment → agentic loop → generate ▲ ▲ └──── everything else stays fixed, so the delta ──────┘ is attributable to what you changed ``` **All eight stages take effect.** Five at query time (`reranker`, `query_enhancer`, `embedder`, `retriever`, `agentic_pipeline`), two at ingest (`chunker` and `document_processor`), and `generator`, which writes the answer from what retrieval returned. In a sweep, every stage but the document processor swaps with a single config key; a chunker or embedder arm gets a corpus of its own, chunked or embedded by its component. Settings (`chunk_size`, `embedding_model` and so on) swap the same way. Benchmark corpora are loaded as text, so a document processor is checked on your own files instead. A swapped stage *replaces* the built-in rather than layering on top of it, so the component being measured is the component that ran. --- ## How Lasagna compares Lasagna is not an alternative to LangChain, LlamaIndex or RAGAS: LangChain and LangGraph are core dependencies, and RAGAS computes the judged generation metrics. It is a layer for measuring which change moved a number. | | **Lasagna** | **LlamaIndex** | **LangChain** | |---|---|---|---| | The job it is for | Knowing *which* change moved the number | Turning messy documents into a usable index | Providers, agents, shipping to production | | Reach for it when | You must defend a result in a paper or review | Your hard problem is PDFs, OCR, tables | Your hard problem is integrations and agents | | Don't, when | You need breadth, stability or a small install | You need statistical rigor about *why* | You want an opinionated, attributable experiment | What it adds is the measurement apparatus: a paired sign-flip test with t intervals, Holm-Bonferroni correction across a sweep (with adjusted p-values), a 2x2 interaction test with a t interval, per-sample scores joined by sample identity, comparability keys that record what was held fixed, a check from what actually ran that two arms differ only in the stages they name, and integrity-checked result bundles. Significance testing itself is not new (PyTerrier and ranx have it for IR runs, UltraRAG has a paired permutation test); what we did not find elsewhere is the combination inside a RAG pipeline framework, from one sweep file. Typed swap points are not new either (LlamaIndex has `BaseNodePostprocessor`, LangChain has `BaseDocumentCompressor`); Lasagna's are reachable from a plain function with one decorator, and `lasagna.from_langchain` and `lasagna.from_llamaindex` wrap components you already have. Against research RAG tools, as of October 2026. "Not found" means we found it in neither the docs nor a code search, not that it is proven absent. | | **Lasagna** | **FlashRAG** | **BERGEN** | **UltraRAG** | **AutoRAG** | **PyTerrier / ranx** | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Significance tests | Paired sign-flip test, Holm, power | Not found | Not found | Paired permutation, no correction | Not found | Yes, IR runs only | | Interaction between components | 2×2 test with CI | Not found | Not found | Not found | Greedy search assumes none | Not found | | Result provenance | Bundles with a validator | Saved configs and scores | Experiment folders | Not found | Trial folders | Not found | | Published methods | 30 of 55 components cite the paper they implement | 23 methods | 20+ retrievers, 4 rerankers | Several baselines | Many modules | IR pipelines | | Ready corpora and indexes | Benchmark loaders, no prebuilt index | Wikipedia + prebuilt index | KILT + prebuilt index | Not found | Not found | Via ir_datasets | | License | Apache-2.0 | MIT | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | Apache-2.0 | MIT (badge) | MPL-2.0 / MIT | **Where the others win.** FlashRAG and BERGEN ship prebuilt indexes and result tables for many published methods, so a baseline costs little to reproduce; Lasagna ships no prebuilt index and none of its own paper's per-query results yet. AutoRAG has a hosted demo, and FlashRAG, UltraRAG and XRAG have visual UIs. LangChain and LlamaIndex have thousands of integrations and years of production use; this is a first release. Install weight: torch and sentence-transformers are core dependencies, about 1.3 GB installed on macOS arm64, and on Linux x86_64 the default PyPI torch pulls CUDA wheels, about 3.2 GB of downloads. Document parsing: LlamaParse handles formats the built-in pypdf and pdfplumber extraction does not. Observability: LangSmith traces every agent step; Lasagna has Prometheus metrics and JSON logs, and nothing like it. --- ## It reproduces published numbers Before you trust a harness with your component, check it on methods whose numbers are already known. On the full SciFact and NFCorpus test sets, Lasagna's built-in components land within 0.002 NDCG@10 of MTEB for the dense models, and within 0.004 of the BEIR paper for BM25 followed by a MiniLM cross-encoder. BM25 is 0.001 and 0.008 below the BEIR paper, which indexed the title and the text as separate fields. Lasagna's BM25 is its own, rank_bm25's Okapi BM25 over one field holding both; like for like, against Anserini's BM25 over one such field, it is 0.015 (SciFact) and 0.005 (NFCorpus) below ([how the two differ](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/reproduction/README.md#notes-on-the-differences)). Nothing was tuned: BM25 uses BEIR's k1 and b, and every model is its published checkpoint. | Method | SciFact published | SciFact Lasagna | NFCorpus published | NFCorpus Lasagna | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | BM25 (k1 0.9, b 0.4) | 0.665 | 0.664 | 0.325 | 0.317 | | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 | 0.645 | 0.645 | 0.316 | 0.317 | | bge-small-en-v1.5 | 0.713 | 0.713 | 0.343 | 0.344 | | BM25 + MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder | 0.688 | 0.685 | 0.350 | 0.351 | NDCG@10. Published: BEIR (Thakur et al., NeurIPS 2021, Table 2) and the MTEB results repository. It reruns in about half an hour on a laptop, with no API key: `lasagna benchmark experiment examples/reproduction/beir_tier1.yaml`. Sources, setup, recall@100 and the remaining BM25 gap are in [examples/reproduction](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/reproduction/README.md). --- ## Quickstart ```bash pip install lasagna-rag ``` Start with the `speed` profile: a 92 MB embedding model, no LLM and no API key. ```python import asyncio from lasagna.sdk import KnowledgeClient, config_for_speed async def main(): # The same session on every run, on the speed profile. client = KnowledgeClient(session_id="quickstart", config=config_for_speed()) doc = await client.upload("paper.pdf") await client.documents.wait_for_processing(doc.document_id) # upload returns once queued results = await client.search_documents("What did the ablation show?") for r in results.results: print(f"[{r.score:.2f}] {r.chunk.content[:120]}") await client.close() asyncio.run(main()) ``` Or from the shell (`lasagna init` asks the same questions interactively): ```bash lasagna configure --profile speed # the speed profile for the default session lasagna upload paper.pdf lasagna search "what did the ablation show?" lasagna serve # REST API and configuration page on 127.0.0.1:8000 ``` > **What the first run takes.** On an Apple M1 Max (10 cores, 64 GB), the > script above printed its first result 30 to 35 seconds after it started with > an empty model cache (the 92 MB download included), and 8 seconds with the > model cached. A search after that took 15 ms (the median of ten, on one > document; release-gate runs measured a 32 ms median over 18,442 chunks on > Milvus Lite). In the shell, each command loads the model and opens the store > again, so a `lasagna search` took about 10 seconds; while `lasagna serve` > runs, the CLI asks the server instead. > > **The default profile is the quality option.** A session with no profile > uses it (leave out `config=` and `--profile`): BGE-M3 embeddings and the > mxbai reranker, **about 3.2 GB downloaded** on the first upload and the first > search that reranks (BGE-M3, 2.3 GB, and the reranker, 881 MB), and > 2.3 GB more with the `flag-embedding` extra (which `[all]` includes), since > FlagEmbedding fetches BGE-M3's whole repository, ONNX export included. On > release-gate runs its first search result took 2–40 minutes on a cold cache; > the spread is the connection. Warm, a search took 117 ms (median) on the same > M1 Max using its GPU, and 3.1 seconds on two CPU threads. The default, > `standard`, `balanced` and `max_quality` profiles send queries they judge > complex to an agentic loop, which calls an LLM; without an API key those > queries run the profile's standard pipeline, and the result's > `degraded_stages` names `agentic`. From a source checkout, > `python -m e2e.run` measures the cold start on your own machine (the `e2e` > package is not in the wheel); with pip, `lasagna doctor` checks what is > installed and cached. > > **Settings belong to a session.** A client's settings are saved as its > session's, and a client without `config=` reads the session's saved > settings, so the CLI, REST API, MCP server and a rerun of this script search > that corpus with the same model. Each session has its own embedding model: > two clients in one process on different sessions can use different models. > [Configuration](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) > explains profiles, which setting wins when several places set it, and where > data is kept (`~/.lasagna`). `upload()` returns as soon as the document is queued; processing is asynchronous, so await `client.documents.wait_for_processing(...)` before searching or reading the final chunk count. It raises `DocumentProcessingError`, with the reason and the fix, if the document could not be indexed. Rerunning the script uploads nothing new: a file the session already holds comes back as that document, with `duplicate_of` set (`allow_duplicates=True`, or `lasagna upload --force`, indexes it again). **The smallest first run.** In the [component comparison](#compare-a-component) below, `python my_ideas.py` downloads nothing, and the sweep downloads 183 MB once: the `speed` profile's embedder and the cross-encoder it is compared against, 92 MB each. Neither needs a dataset or an API key. It is the fastest way to see what this library is for. --- ## Give your agent RAG: MCP, REST, Docker The MCP server and the REST API run the same retrieval pipeline, profiles and settings that the benchmarks measure, so a profile or setting that won your comparison is what your agent searches with. ### MCP: a search tool for Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor ```bash pip install lasagna-rag lasagna configure --profile speed -s my-corpus # 92 MB model, no API key lasagna upload ./docs/*.md -s my-corpus # several files, one model load ``` Then register the server. **Claude Code**: `.mcp.json` in your project. **Claude Desktop**: the same block inside `claude_desktop_config.json`. ```json { "mcpServers": { "lasagna": { "command": "lasagna-mcp", "env": { "RAG_SESSION_ID": "my-corpus" } } } } ``` `lasagna-mcp` speaks stdio, which is how these clients launch a server; if it is not on the client's `PATH`, give the absolute path inside your virtualenv. The server has 29 tools (search, upload, document lifecycle, profiles and configuration). By default it serves the `safe` set, 22 tools: it leaves out the seven that delete documents, profiles or collections, reset a session's configuration or change the server-wide retention policy; `--tools all` serves all 29. A tool acts on the session `RAG_SESSION_ID` names unless its `session_id` argument names another. `--transport sse` serves a port for several clients at once. The [MCP guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/mcp/README.md) lists every tool. ### REST API ```bash lasagna serve # http://127.0.0.1:8000, loopback only ``` ```bash curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/search \ -H "X-Session-ID: my-corpus" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "what did the ablation show?", "top_k": 5}' ``` The OpenAPI reference is at `/docs`, and every endpoint is listed in [endpoints.md](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/api/docs/endpoints.md). `lasagna serve` binds to loopback and is unauthenticated; for anything shared, use the Compose stack. A local store opens in one process at a time. While `lasagna serve` runs, `lasagna status`, `search`, `upload` and `configure` go through it, and `lasagna-mcp` cannot open the store. To give an agent the same store, start the server with the MCP endpoint and register it by URL instead of the command: ```bash lasagna serve --mcp -s my-corpus # REST API, and MCP over SSE at /mcp/sse ``` `-s` names the session that MCP tool calls and REST requests use when they name none; without it, MCP tools must pass `session_id`. ```json { "mcpServers": { "lasagna": { "type": "sse", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/sse" } } } ``` ### Docker Compose [`src/lasagna/deploy/`](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/deploy/README.md) runs Lasagna as a service with `make up`: the API behind Gunicorn, signed session tokens issued against API keys, PostgreSQL for metadata, Redis, Celery workers for ingestion, the MCP server, Prometheus metrics and a readiness check. A Milvus server is the default vector store, and each of the six backends has a compose fragment (`make up VECTOR_BACKEND=pgvector`). Request sizes and search time are bounded, and uploads are shared between the API, the worker and the MCP server. ### Skills, so the agent stops guessing ```bash lasagna skills install # writes .claude/skills/ lasagna doctor # what is wrong with this install, and how to fix it lasagna doctor --issue # a redacted block to paste into a bug report ``` Four skills: using retrieval, building a component, running an evaluation, and filing a useful bug report. They encode what an agent otherwise gets wrong: which mode a benchmark must run in, why the first search is slow, and which config applies. --- ## Compare a component > **Run it on a real benchmark:** [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/notebooks/compare_your_reranker.ipynb) > One notebook writes a reranker as a single function, sweeps it against a > built-in cross-encoder on 100 SciFact queries over the full corpus, and ends > with a paired significance test, the stage isolation check and a validated > results bundle. No API key. It is stored without outputs: run it on Colab, or > locally with Jupyter, to see them. Adding a technique is one decorator on a plain function. The function becomes a component of its stage, interchangeable with every built-in, and runs inside the complete pipeline. Save this as `my_ideas.py`; `python my_ideas.py` runs as is, with no model download and no corpus: ```python # my_ideas.py import lasagna @lasagna.reranker(paper="Doe et al. 2026", claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.456}}) def keyword_overlap(query, text): # your technique: score one passage return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split())) if __name__ == "__main__": # try it on three passages from lasagna.core.base_components import ScoredDocument from lasagna.core.registry import registry candidates = [ ScoredDocument(content="short", score=0.9, document_id="d1", chunk_id="c1"), ScoredDocument(content="a considerably longer passage of text", score=0.5, document_id="d2", chunk_id="c2"), ScoredDocument(content="middling length here", score=0.7, document_id="d3", chunk_id="c3"), ] mine = registry.get("reranker", "keyword_overlap").rerank("length of a passage", candidates) entry = next(e for e in registry.list_rerankers() if e["name"] == "keyword_overlap") print("retrieval order:", [d.document_id for d in candidates]) print("my reranker: ", [d.document_id for d in mine]) print("claims recorded:", entry["claims"]) print("interchangeable:", entry["implements_contract"]) ``` ```text retrieval order: ['d1', 'd2', 'd3'] my reranker: ['d2', 'd3', 'd1'] claims recorded: {'beir/scifact': {'ndcg@10': 0.456}} interchangeable: True ``` `paper` and `claims` travel with the component and come back out of the registry. A claim names the benchmark the paper measured it on (and its split, as `"split": "test"`, if the paper gives one). A run records them (`components` in its metadata and its bundle), and on a run of that benchmark the leaderboard `benchmark experiment` prints, `results leaderboard` (markdown and LaTeX) and `results view` put the claimed number and its paper beside the one you reproduced. The smoke sweep below shows no claim, since the paper did not measure smoke. Every stage but the agentic pipeline takes a function the same way: `@lasagna.query_enhancer` (`query -> [str]`), `@lasagna.chunker` (`text -> [str]`), `@lasagna.embedder` (`texts -> vectors`), `@lasagna.generator` (`query, contexts -> answer`), `@lasagna.retriever` and `@lasagna.document_processor`. A reranker can also order the whole list (`query, documents, top_k`). The function is handed copies, so it cannot change what another stage sees. When a technique needs state or a model, or is an agentic loop, subclass the stage's interface (`BaseReranker`, `BaseAgenticPipeline` and so on) and register the class with `@registry.register` instead. Then measure it. A sweep names the function by its import path, `my_ideas:keyword_overlap`, with no registration call and no package: ```yaml # sweep.yaml, next to my_ideas.py name: does keyword_overlap help benchmarks: [{name: smoke}] tracks: [retrieval] pipeline: base_profile: speed rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"] n_runs: 1 # retrieval does not sample; repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop ``` ```bash lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml # downloads 183 MB of models the first time lasagna results significance "/results.json" -m ndcg@10 --all ``` Before any corpus is ingested, the run checks that each named component implements its stage and passes its behavioral contract (return types, `top_k`, empty input, no mutation of its input). It then runs both arms on the same queries and ends by confirming that the configuration reaching each stage differed only at the reranker, and that the reranker arm's ranked lists moved: an arm whose lists never moved is flagged inert, and so is a reranker that hands back its candidates in retrieval order on every query, with no reranker-free arm needed to compare against (on fewer than ten queries it says there were too few to tell). Every listed built-in implements its stage's interface, so any of them is a like-for-like control: ```python from lasagna.core.registry import registry [r["name"] for r in registry.list_rerankers() if r["implements_contract"]] # ['cross_encoder', 'combined', 'ensemble', 'mmr', 'colbert', 'llm_listwise', # 'monot5', 'llm_pointwise', 'flashrank', 'cohere'] ``` [The guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md#8-measure-it-on-a-benchmark) covers the 32 benchmarks, your own data, baseline arms (`closed_book`, `long_context`, `no_rag: true`), `--dry-run` with a cost estimate, the LLM response cache, and how to read, view and publish a result. ### Why the stages stay isolated A comparison is attributable only if the arms differ in the stage under test and nowhere else. Lasagna checks that rather than assuming it. - **A fixed interface per stage.** Components exchange only their stage's declared types, and function components get copies of what they are handed. A conformance suite checks that every registered component subclasses its stage's contract, does not mutate its input, and does not hand out chunks that share one metadata dict. From a source checkout (the tests are not in the wheel), run `pytest tests/test_abc_conformance.py tests/test_stage_isolation_behavioural.py`. - **A stage manifest per task.** Each run records what reached each of the eight stages: every setting, from the configuration the search actually resolved, and the component in the slot. - **A check across arms.** If two arms differ at a stage neither of them names, the run says so, the bundle is marked `UNDECLARED_STAGE_CHANGE`, and `lasagna results validate` refuses it, naming the stage and the settings that moved. An arm whose named change never reached its stage is flagged as inert, since its number is the control's under another name. ### Do two techniques compose, or do they overlap? The question two papers cannot answer between them. Hybrid search is published against a dense baseline; reranking is published against a baseline. Whether hybrid search still helps once a reranker is on does not follow from those two numbers: both may fix the same queries. Answering it needs all four cells measured on the same queries. Declare the 2×2 and the harness builds them: ```yaml # compose.yaml name: hybrid search with reranking benchmarks: - name: beir/scifact n_samples: 100 tracks: [retrieval] pipeline: base_profile: speed factorial: factor_a: enable_hybrid_search factor_b: enable_reranking ``` ```bash lasagna benchmark experiment compose.yaml lasagna results interaction "/results.json" --metric ndcg@10 ``` This one is keyless: `speed` embeds with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, BM25 needs no model, and reranking turned on uses the 92 MB MiniLM cross-encoder. A real run on 100 SciFact queries printed: ```text Cells 'reranking' and 'hybrid_search+reranking' returned identical ranked lists on all 100 shared queries. If the factor that separates them acts on retrieval, it did nothing in that cell, and the interaction below reflects that rather than an overlap between the techniques. expected if additive : -0.0081 actually observed : -0.0062 interaction : +0.0019 95% CI [-0.0318, +0.0355] p=0.9141 composition efficiency: not reported because the interaction is not significant (p=0.9141), so the ratio would describe noise additive (no detectable interaction) ``` On this corpus neither technique helped the dense baseline, and once the reranker was on, hybrid search changed none of the top ten. It was not skipped: it reordered the candidates, and that is all it could do here. Each cell asks for 40 chunks (ten documents, over-fetched four times), and `enable_hybrid_search` fuses the dense and BM25 lists by weighted rank, with `hybrid_alpha` 0.7 and `rrf_k` 60. A chunk only BM25 finds scores at most 0.3/60 = 0.0050, below the 40th dense chunk's 0.7/99 = 0.0071, so the fused 40 are the dense 40 in another order; on all 100 queries the reranker was handed the same 40 chunks in both cells. The cross-encoder scores each chunk on its own, so it returned the same top ten. For BM25 to bring in chunks of its own at this depth, `hybrid_alpha` must be below 0.62, or sweep the `hybrid_rrf` retriever, which fuses each list's top `hybrid_fusion_depth` (1,000) unweighted. The harness says so instead of reporting a 2×2 that only looks complete. The statistic is `(AB − neither) − (A − neither) − (B − neither)`, tested by sign-flipping each query's interaction contrast (all four cells of a query move together), with a t interval. Positive means the techniques compound; negative means they overlap. Factors are boolean settings, not component names: a component slot has no *off* level for the `neither` cell, and a factorial over anything else is refused before the first corpus is ingested. --- ## What's inside ### Pluggable RAG pipeline stages | Stage | Registered | Notes | |---|---:|---| | `retriever` | 5 | dense, BM25, SPLADE, hybrid RRF, hybrid convex (normalized score fusion) | | `reranker` | 10 | cross-encoder (any Hugging Face reranker, e.g. bge-reranker-v2-m3), ColBERT, monoT5, RankGPT listwise, LLM pointwise, FlashRank, Cohere Rerank, MMR, ensemble, combined | | `query_enhancer` | 8 | HyDE, Query2doc, step-back, Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, RAG-Fusion multi-query, expansion, least-to-most decomposition, combined | | `agentic_pipeline` | 7 | default graph (CRAG grading, Self-RAG-style gates, multi-hop planning), Self-Ask, IRCoT, FLARE, Adaptive-RAG, Self-RAG, legacy ReAct | | `generator` | 6 | concise, cited (ALCE), chain-of-thought, chain-of-note, closed-book, long-context | | `chunker` | 9 | fixed (characters, words or tokens), recursive, sentence window, Markdown header, semantic (Kamradt breakpoints), hierarchical, structure-aware, propositions (Dense X), contextual (Contextual Retrieval) | | `embedder` | 6 | any sentence-transformers model with its model card's prefixes, BGE-M3, OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, and the configured default | | `document_processor` | 4 | built-in (pypdf, pdfplumber, OCR), Docling, MarkItDown, PyMuPDF4LLM | `lasagna component list` prints them with each one's paper. Matryoshka truncation, late chunking, lost-in-the-middle reordering, context compression and speculative RAG are settings, and sweep the same way. ### Vector databases: six backends, one interface Milvus · pgvector · Qdrant · Weaviate · Pinecone · OpenSearch, behind one interface with a shared conformance suite asserting the same behavior against each. CI runs it on every pull request against Milvus Lite and Qdrant's local mode, which run in-process; the others need their service running ([details](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/vector_backends/README.md)). Each embedding model gets a vector collection of its own, so sessions on different profiles never mix vectors. ### RAG evaluation: 32 benchmarks, retrieval and generation metrics 32 benchmark entries over about 22 datasets (BEIR, RAGBench and KILT subsets count separately; `lasagna benchmark list` also shows `smoke`, a 24-document wiring check that is not counted, and any benchmark a plugin adds): BEIR (NFCorpus, FiQA, SciFact, ArguAna, HotpotQA), HotpotQA, SQuAD v2, MuSiQue, TriviaQA, Natural Questions, MS MARCO, FEVER, PopQA, Bamboogle, MultiHop-RAG, RAGBench, KILT, 2WikiMultihop. Your own JSONL, CSV or BEIR folder runs with no adapter ([own data](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/own-data.md)). `2wikimultihopqa` adds retrieval over the validation split's full contexts, including distractors, alongside the existing generation-only `wiki_multihop` entry. It reads the Apache-2.0 [official mirror](https://huggingface.co/datasets/xanhho/2WikiMultihopQA) at a fixed revision. Paragraph identity collapses whitespace and removes spacing around punctuation/symbols, preserving case and all non-whitespace characters. The exact rule first applies `" ".join(text.split())`, then `re.sub(r"\s*([^\w\s])\s*", r"\1", text)` before hashing. The first version of a title uses the title as its document ID; other versions add a stable hash of that normalized text. Formatting copies share one ID and the first original text is stored unchanged, giving 55,020 validation documents. `validation` is the default. `train` can be loaded as samples, but `load_corpus()` always supplies validation's corpus, so use `--split validation` for retrieval evaluation. | Family | Metrics | |---|---| | Retrieval | NDCG@k, precision@k, recall@k, F1@k, hit rate (success)@k, MAP, MRR, R-precision, complete (all-gold) recall@k for multi-hop questions | | Generation, no judge | exact match and token F1 (SQuAD-normalized; SQuAD v2 scored answerable and unanswerable separately), ROUGE-L, answer containment, answer similarity (embedding), abstention rate | | Generation, judged | faithfulness, context precision, context recall, factual correctness (RAGAS); citation recall and precision (ALCE) when answers cite; opt-in: answer relevancy, noise sensitivity, context relevance | | Operational | p50/p95/p99 latency (retrieval and generation, end to end), input and output tokens and LLM calls per query, with the judge's spend reported separately | Plus multi-objective tradeoff analysis, paired significance testing, and t confidence intervals. ### Interfaces and profiles Python SDK · REST API · MCP server · CLI · schema-driven configuration page. Five profiles: `default` (the settings file) and four presets, from `speed` (dense vector search only, keyless) through `standard` and `balanced` to `max_quality` (every retrieval feature on; the paper calls it Max-Reliable). `speed` turns off reranking, hybrid search, MMR, HyDE and the agentic loop. [Configuration](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#profiles) lists what each one runs and downloads. --- ## Install ```bash pip install lasagna-rag # core: ingest, embed, search, serve python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab # once: nltk's sentence tokenizer data ``` Lasagna supports Python 3.10 to 3.13. To reproduce a result exactly, install the versions the release was tested with. That constraints file was resolved on Python 3.12 and needs 3.12 or later (its numpy does not install on 3.10 or 3.11): ```bash pip install "lasagna-rag[eval]==0.1.0" -c https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dolev31/lasagna/v0.1.0/constraints/0.1.0.txt ``` `eval` adds the RAGAS metrics, benchmark loaders and statistics; the other extras (vector backends, document processors, LLM providers, the production stack) and the platform notes (CPU-only torch on Linux, Apple Silicon) are in [the guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md#2-install). `pip install lasagna` installs a different project; this one is `lasagna-rag`. Lasagna collects no usage telemetry, and turns off the usage events ragas would otherwise send (`RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=true`, unless you set it yourself). --- ## Model licenses Lasagna ships **no model weights**. They download from their upstream host on first use, each under its own license. Four selectable models are **not licensed for commercial use** (or state no license), including `naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil`, the default SPLADE sparse encoder, and `castorini/monot5-base-msmarco-10k`, the default monoT5 reranker; selecting one logs a warning naming the license. Before taking a configuration into a commercial product, read **[docs/model-licenses.md](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/model-licenses.md)**. ```python from lasagna.core.model_licenses import is_commercial_use_restricted is_commercial_use_restricted("naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil") # True ``` Benchmark corpora are never redistributed: they are fetched from their official sources and carry their own terms (`lasagna benchmark licenses`). --- ## Testing ```bash pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/live --ignore=tests/stress ``` Hermetic by default: no network, no external services, and the suite runs in a throwaway home directory, so it never touches your real `~/.lasagna` store. CI enforces it: sockets are blocked except loopback, and test order is shuffled on every run (pytest-randomly prints the seed). `tests/live/` needs a running stack; `tests/stress/` is long-running. Coverage is measured with branches on and floored in CI. --- ## Documentation **Start here: [Working with Lasagna](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md)**: install, write a component, compare it against a baseline, measure it on a benchmark, and publish the result. Every Python example in it is executed by the release gate on each run. | I want to... | Read | |---|---| | Measure a component, or run a sweep | licenses](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/knowledge_evaluation_sdk/research/DATASETS.md) · [Citation](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/CITATION.cff) Each package directory has a short README for contributors, next to the code it describes. The guide, this README and `CONTRIBUTING.md` have their examples executed by the release gate; report anything elsewhere that does not work. --- ## The paper Lasagna is the framework behind **[Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)** ([Ido Levy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/idolevi31/), [Segev Shlomov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/segev-shlomov/), [Leshem Choshen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leshemchoshen/), 2026). The study tests 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora from 5K to 200K documents, and asks whether gains measured one component at a time survive when the components are combined.

| What the study found | Predicted | Realized | |---|---|---| | Retrieval gains do not add up: the three strongest single techniques, combined (NDCG@10) | +47% | +17% | | Faithfulness gains do carry over: one factor at a time versus the best full pipeline | +28% | +32% | **The best pipeline also changes with corpus size.** At 200K documents, the design that leads at small corpora trails by 13.7% NDCG@10, with the rank flip visible from 25K. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722) · [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29722) · [Project page](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/) · [Explainer video](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#explainer) · [Podcast (AI-generated, 25 min)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#podcast) · [Pre-registration](https://github.com/dolev31/Lasagna-Retrieval-Augmented-Generation-Compositionality) ### Citing Lasagna If you publish work that uses Lasagna, please cite it: see [CITATION.cff](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/CITATION.cff), which GitHub renders as a ready-made BibTeX entry. To cite the paper: ```bibtex @misc{levy2026retrieval, title = {Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality}, author = {Levy, Ido and Shlomov, Segev and Choshen, Leshem}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2610.29722}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.CL}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722} } ``` If you also report a number from the evaluation harness, publish the results bundle with it: ```bash lasagna results bundle -o run.json ``` It carries the library versions, hardware, resolved sweep, corpus fingerprint and comparability key: what a reader needs to decide whether your number and theirs measure the same thing. `lasagna results validate` recomputes the key, the run id and every aggregate from its per-query scores, so a number edited after the run no longer matches its bundle. That is an integrity check against mistakes and naive edits, not a signature: anyone who edits a number can recompute the id, which is why the hub's trust model calls results self-reported. [hub/](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/tree/main/hub) has what is needed to run a public leaderboard for bundles: a generated JSON Schema, a pull-request validation workflow, and that trust model. --- ## License Apache 2.0: see [LICENSE](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/LICENSE) and [NOTICE](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/NOTICE). Lasagna vendors no third-party source code.

**Test your RAG components against a real stack, not a toy baseline. Then give that stack to your agent.** Code for **[Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)**
[Ido Levy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/idolevi31/)1,2 · [Segev Shlomov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/segev-shlomov/)1 · [Leshem Choshen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leshemchoshen/)1,2
1IBM · 2Weizmann Institute of Science [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.29722-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722) [![Project page](https://img.shields.io/badge/project-page-1f6feb.svg)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-read-1f6feb.svg)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/docs/) [![Podcast](https://img.shields.io/badge/podcast-25_min-1f6feb.svg?logo=data%3Aimage%2Fsvg%2Bxml%3Bbase64%%3D%3D)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#podcast) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/lasagna-rag.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/lasagna-rag/) [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/1428808706.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23548068) [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/LICENSE) [![Python 3.10 to 3.13](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%20|%203.11%20|%203.12%20|%203.13-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![Tests](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/actions/workflows/tests.yml) [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/notebooks/compare_your_reranker.ipynb) **[Quickstart](#quickstart)** · **[Compare a component](#compare-a-component)** · **[Give your agent RAG](#give-your-agent-rag-mcp-rest-docker)** · **[Docs](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/docs/)** · **[The paper](#the-paper)**


A real run with the idle waits cut: write a reranker, sweep it against a built-in, and get a Holm-corrected verdict.

| You want to | Start here | |---|---| | Show that your component helps, with a significance test and no API key | [Compare a component](#compare-a-component) | | Give an agent search over your own documents (MCP, REST, Docker) | [Give your agent RAG](#give-your-agent-rag-mcp-rest-docker) | | Pick a vector backend and retrieval strategy without building a harness | [Quickstart](#quickstart), then [What's inside](#whats-inside) | | Read what the paper found | [The paper](#the-paper) | --- ## The problem Most RAG results are reported one component at a time. A new reranker is measured against a baseline with no query augmentation, no agentic loop, and an old chunker, because building the rest of the stack just to run the comparison is more work than the contribution itself. That makes published gains hard to add up. If a reranker claims +4 NDCG and a query expander claims +3, you cannot tell from the papers whether stacking them gives you **+7, +4, or -1**. Lasagna exists to make that question answerable. ``` ┌─────────── your component drops in here ───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → rerank → augment → agentic loop → generate ▲ ▲ └──── everything else stays fixed, so the delta ──────┘ is attributable to what you changed ``` **All eight stages take effect.** Five at query time (`reranker`, `query_enhancer`, `embedder`, `retriever`, `agentic_pipeline`), two at ingest (`chunker` and `document_processor`), and `generator`, which writes the answer from what retrieval returned. In a sweep, every stage but the document processor swaps with a single config key; a chunker or embedder arm gets a corpus of its own, chunked or embedded by its component. Settings (`chunk_size`, `embedding_model` and so on) swap the same way. Benchmark corpora are loaded as text, so a document processor is checked on your own files instead. A swapped stage *replaces* the built-in rather than layering on top of it, so the component being measured is the component that ran. --- ## How Lasagna compares Lasagna is not an alternative to LangChain, LlamaIndex or RAGAS: LangChain and LangGraph are core dependencies, and RAGAS computes the judged generation metrics. It is a layer for measuring which change moved a number. | | **Lasagna** | **LlamaIndex** | **LangChain** | |---|---|---|---| | The job it is for | Knowing *which* change moved the number | Turning messy documents into a usable index | Providers, agents, shipping to production | | Reach for it when | You must defend a result in a paper or review | Your hard problem is PDFs, OCR, tables | Your hard problem is integrations and agents | | Don't, when | You need breadth, stability or a small install | You need statistical rigor about *why* | You want an opinionated, attributable experiment | What it adds is the measurement apparatus: a paired sign-flip test with t intervals, Holm-Bonferroni correction across a sweep (with adjusted p-values), a 2x2 interaction test with a t interval, per-sample scores joined by sample identity, comparability keys that record what was held fixed, a check from what actually ran that two arms differ only in the stages they name, and integrity-checked result bundles. Significance testing itself is not new (PyTerrier and ranx have it for IR runs, UltraRAG has a paired permutation test); what we did not find elsewhere is the combination inside a RAG pipeline framework, from one sweep file. Typed swap points are not new either (LlamaIndex has `BaseNodePostprocessor`, LangChain has `BaseDocumentCompressor`); Lasagna's are reachable from a plain function with one decorator, and `lasagna.from_langchain` and `lasagna.from_llamaindex` wrap components you already have. Against research RAG tools, as of October 2026. "Not found" means we found it in neither the docs nor a code search, not that it is proven absent. | | **Lasagna** | **FlashRAG** | **BERGEN** | **UltraRAG** | **AutoRAG** | **PyTerrier / ranx** | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Significance tests | Paired sign-flip test, Holm, power | Not found | Not found | Paired permutation, no correction | Not found | Yes, IR runs only | | Interaction between components | 2×2 test with CI | Not found | Not found | Not found | Greedy search assumes none | Not found | | Result provenance | Bundles with a validator | Saved configs and scores | Experiment folders | Not found | Trial folders | Not found | | Published methods | 30 of 55 components cite the paper they implement | 23 methods | 20+ retrievers, 4 rerankers | Several baselines | Many modules | IR pipelines | | Ready corpora and indexes | Benchmark loaders, no prebuilt index | Wikipedia + prebuilt index | KILT + prebuilt index | Not found | Not found | Via ir_datasets | | License | Apache-2.0 | MIT | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | Apache-2.0 | MIT (badge) | MPL-2.0 / MIT | **Where the others win.** FlashRAG and BERGEN ship prebuilt indexes and result tables for many published methods, so a baseline costs little to reproduce; Lasagna ships no prebuilt index and none of its own paper's per-query results yet. AutoRAG has a hosted demo, and FlashRAG, UltraRAG and XRAG have visual UIs. LangChain and LlamaIndex have thousands of integrations and years of production use; this is a first release. Install weight: torch and sentence-transformers are core dependencies, about 1.3 GB installed on macOS arm64, and on Linux x86_64 the default PyPI torch pulls CUDA wheels, about 3.2 GB of downloads. Document parsing: LlamaParse handles formats the built-in pypdf and pdfplumber extraction does not. Observability: LangSmith traces every agent step; Lasagna has Prometheus metrics and JSON logs, and nothing like it. --- ## It reproduces published numbers Before you trust a harness with your component, check it on methods whose numbers are already known. On the full SciFact and NFCorpus test sets, Lasagna's built-in components land within 0.002 NDCG@10 of MTEB for the dense models, and within 0.004 of the BEIR paper for BM25 followed by a MiniLM cross-encoder. BM25 is 0.001 and 0.008 below the BEIR paper, which indexed the title and the text as separate fields. Lasagna's BM25 is its own, rank_bm25's Okapi BM25 over one field holding both; like for like, against Anserini's BM25 over one such field, it is 0.015 (SciFact) and 0.005 (NFCorpus) below ([how the two differ](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/reproduction/README.md#notes-on-the-differences)). Nothing was tuned: BM25 uses BEIR's k1 and b, and every model is its published checkpoint. | Method | SciFact published | SciFact Lasagna | NFCorpus published | NFCorpus Lasagna | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | BM25 (k1 0.9, b 0.4) | 0.665 | 0.664 | 0.325 | 0.317 | | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 | 0.645 | 0.645 | 0.316 | 0.317 | | bge-small-en-v1.5 | 0.713 | 0.713 | 0.343 | 0.344 | | BM25 + MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder | 0.688 | 0.685 | 0.350 | 0.351 | NDCG@10. Published: BEIR (Thakur et al., NeurIPS 2021, Table 2) and the MTEB results repository. It reruns in about half an hour on a laptop, with no API key: `lasagna benchmark experiment examples/reproduction/beir_tier1.yaml`. Sources, setup, recall@100 and the remaining BM25 gap are in [examples/reproduction](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/reproduction/README.md). --- ## Quickstart ```bash pip install lasagna-rag ``` Start with the `speed` profile: a 92 MB embedding model, no LLM and no API key. ```python import asyncio from lasagna.sdk import KnowledgeClient, config_for_speed async def main(): # The same session on every run, on the speed profile. client = KnowledgeClient(session_id="quickstart", config=config_for_speed()) doc = await client.upload("paper.pdf") await client.documents.wait_for_processing(doc.document_id) # upload returns once queued results = await client.search_documents("What did the ablation show?") for r in results.results: print(f"[{r.score:.2f}] {r.chunk.content[:120]}") await client.close() asyncio.run(main()) ``` Or from the shell (`lasagna init` asks the same questions interactively): ```bash lasagna configure --profile speed # the speed profile for the default session lasagna upload paper.pdf lasagna search "what did the ablation show?" lasagna serve # REST API and configuration page on 127.0.0.1:8000 ``` > **What the first run takes.** On an Apple M1 Max (10 cores, 64 GB), the > script above printed its first result 30 to 35 seconds after it started with > an empty model cache (the 92 MB download included), and 8 seconds with the > model cached. A search after that took 15 ms (the median of ten, on one > document; release-gate runs measured a 32 ms median over 18,442 chunks on > Milvus Lite). In the shell, each command loads the model and opens the store > again, so a `lasagna search` took about 10 seconds; while `lasagna serve` > runs, the CLI asks the server instead. > > **The default profile is the quality option.** A session with no profile > uses it (leave out `config=` and `--profile`): BGE-M3 embeddings and the > mxbai reranker, **about 3.2 GB downloaded** on the first upload and the first > search that reranks (BGE-M3, 2.3 GB, and the reranker, 881 MB), and > 2.3 GB more with the `flag-embedding` extra (which `[all]` includes), since > FlagEmbedding fetches BGE-M3's whole repository, ONNX export included. On > release-gate runs its first search result took 2–40 minutes on a cold cache; > the spread is the connection. Warm, a search took 117 ms (median) on the same > M1 Max using its GPU, and 3.1 seconds on two CPU threads. The default, > `standard`, `balanced` and `max_quality` profiles send queries they judge > complex to an agentic loop, which calls an LLM; without an API key those > queries run the profile's standard pipeline, and the result's > `degraded_stages` names `agentic`. From a source checkout, > `python -m e2e.run` measures the cold start on your own machine (the `e2e` > package is not in the wheel); with pip, `lasagna doctor` checks what is > installed and cached. > > **Settings belong to a session.** A client's settings are saved as its > session's, and a client without `config=` reads the session's saved > settings, so the CLI, REST API, MCP server and a rerun of this script search > that corpus with the same model. Each session has its own embedding model: > two clients in one process on different sessions can use different models. > [Configuration](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) > explains profiles, which setting wins when several places set it, and where > data is kept (`~/.lasagna`). `upload()` returns as soon as the document is queued; processing is asynchronous, so await `client.documents.wait_for_processing(...)` before searching or reading the final chunk count. It raises `DocumentProcessingError`, with the reason and the fix, if the document could not be indexed. Rerunning the script uploads nothing new: a file the session already holds comes back as that document, with `duplicate_of` set (`allow_duplicates=True`, or `lasagna upload --force`, indexes it again). **The smallest first run.** In the [component comparison](#compare-a-component) below, `python my_ideas.py` downloads nothing, and the sweep downloads 183 MB once: the `speed` profile's embedder and the cross-encoder it is compared against, 92 MB each. Neither needs a dataset or an API key. It is the fastest way to see what this library is for. --- ## Give your agent RAG: MCP, REST, Docker The MCP server and the REST API run the same retrieval pipeline, profiles and settings that the benchmarks measure, so a profile or setting that won your comparison is what your agent searches with. ### MCP: a search tool for Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor ```bash pip install lasagna-rag lasagna configure --profile speed -s my-corpus # 92 MB model, no API key lasagna upload ./docs/*.md -s my-corpus # several files, one model load ``` Then register the server. **Claude Code**: `.mcp.json` in your project. **Claude Desktop**: the same block inside `claude_desktop_config.json`. ```json { "mcpServers": { "lasagna": { "command": "lasagna-mcp", "env": { "RAG_SESSION_ID": "my-corpus" } } } } ``` `lasagna-mcp` speaks stdio, which is how these clients launch a server; if it is not on the client's `PATH`, give the absolute path inside your virtualenv. The server has 29 tools (search, upload, document lifecycle, profiles and configuration). By default it serves the `safe` set, 22 tools: it leaves out the seven that delete documents, profiles or collections, reset a session's configuration or change the server-wide retention policy; `--tools all` serves all 29. A tool acts on the session `RAG_SESSION_ID` names unless its `session_id` argument names another. `--transport sse` serves a port for several clients at once. The [MCP guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/mcp/README.md) lists every tool. ### REST API ```bash lasagna serve # http://127.0.0.1:8000, loopback only ``` ```bash curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/search \ -H "X-Session-ID: my-corpus" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"query": "what did the ablation show?", "top_k": 5}' ``` The OpenAPI reference is at `/docs`, and every endpoint is listed in [endpoints.md](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/api/docs/endpoints.md). `lasagna serve` binds to loopback and is unauthenticated; for anything shared, use the Compose stack. A local store opens in one process at a time. While `lasagna serve` runs, `lasagna status`, `search`, `upload` and `configure` go through it, and `lasagna-mcp` cannot open the store. To give an agent the same store, start the server with the MCP endpoint and register it by URL instead of the command: ```bash lasagna serve --mcp -s my-corpus # REST API, and MCP over SSE at /mcp/sse ``` `-s` names the session that MCP tool calls and REST requests use when they name none; without it, MCP tools must pass `session_id`. ```json { "mcpServers": { "lasagna": { "type": "sse", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/sse" } } } ``` ### Docker Compose [`src/lasagna/deploy/`](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/deploy/README.md) runs Lasagna as a service with `make up`: the API behind Gunicorn, signed session tokens issued against API keys, PostgreSQL for metadata, Redis, Celery workers for ingestion, the MCP server, Prometheus metrics and a readiness check. A Milvus server is the default vector store, and each of the six backends has a compose fragment (`make up VECTOR_BACKEND=pgvector`). Request sizes and search time are bounded, and uploads are shared between the API, the worker and the MCP server. ### Skills, so the agent stops guessing ```bash lasagna skills install # writes .claude/skills/ lasagna doctor # what is wrong with this install, and how to fix it lasagna doctor --issue # a redacted block to paste into a bug report ``` Four skills: using retrieval, building a component, running an evaluation, and filing a useful bug report. They encode what an agent otherwise gets wrong: which mode a benchmark must run in, why the first search is slow, and which config applies. --- ## Compare a component > **Run it on a real benchmark:** [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/examples/notebooks/compare_your_reranker.ipynb) > One notebook writes a reranker as a single function, sweeps it against a > built-in cross-encoder on 100 SciFact queries over the full corpus, and ends > with a paired significance test, the stage isolation check and a validated > results bundle. No API key. It is stored without outputs: run it on Colab, or > locally with Jupyter, to see them. Adding a technique is one decorator on a plain function. The function becomes a component of its stage, interchangeable with every built-in, and runs inside the complete pipeline. Save this as `my_ideas.py`; `python my_ideas.py` runs as is, with no model download and no corpus: ```python # my_ideas.py import lasagna @lasagna.reranker(paper="Doe et al. 2026", claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.456}}) def keyword_overlap(query, text): # your technique: score one passage return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split())) if __name__ == "__main__": # try it on three passages from lasagna.core.base_components import ScoredDocument from lasagna.core.registry import registry candidates = [ ScoredDocument(content="short", score=0.9, document_id="d1", chunk_id="c1"), ScoredDocument(content="a considerably longer passage of text", score=0.5, document_id="d2", chunk_id="c2"), ScoredDocument(content="middling length here", score=0.7, document_id="d3", chunk_id="c3"), ] mine = registry.get("reranker", "keyword_overlap").rerank("length of a passage", candidates) entry = next(e for e in registry.list_rerankers() if e["name"] == "keyword_overlap") print("retrieval order:", [d.document_id for d in candidates]) print("my reranker: ", [d.document_id for d in mine]) print("claims recorded:", entry["claims"]) print("interchangeable:", entry["implements_contract"]) ``` ```text retrieval order: ['d1', 'd2', 'd3'] my reranker: ['d2', 'd3', 'd1'] claims recorded: {'beir/scifact': {'ndcg@10': 0.456}} interchangeable: True ``` `paper` and `claims` travel with the component and come back out of the registry. A claim names the benchmark the paper measured it on (and its split, as `"split": "test"`, if the paper gives one). A run records them (`components` in its metadata and its bundle), and on a run of that benchmark the leaderboard `benchmark experiment` prints, `results leaderboard` (markdown and LaTeX) and `results view` put the claimed number and its paper beside the one you reproduced. The smoke sweep below shows no claim, since the paper did not measure smoke. Every stage but the agentic pipeline takes a function the same way: `@lasagna.query_enhancer` (`query -> [str]`), `@lasagna.chunker` (`text -> [str]`), `@lasagna.embedder` (`texts -> vectors`), `@lasagna.generator` (`query, contexts -> answer`), `@lasagna.retriever` and `@lasagna.document_processor`. A reranker can also order the whole list (`query, documents, top_k`). The function is handed copies, so it cannot change what another stage sees. When a technique needs state or a model, or is an agentic loop, subclass the stage's interface (`BaseReranker`, `BaseAgenticPipeline` and so on) and register the class with `@registry.register` instead. Then measure it. A sweep names the function by its import path, `my_ideas:keyword_overlap`, with no registration call and no package: ```yaml # sweep.yaml, next to my_ideas.py name: does keyword_overlap help benchmarks: [{name: smoke}] tracks: [retrieval] pipeline: base_profile: speed rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"] n_runs: 1 # retrieval does not sample; repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop ``` ```bash lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml # downloads 183 MB of models the first time lasagna results significance "/results.json" -m ndcg@10 --all ``` Before any corpus is ingested, the run checks that each named component implements its stage and passes its behavioral contract (return types, `top_k`, empty input, no mutation of its input). It then runs both arms on the same queries and ends by confirming that the configuration reaching each stage differed only at the reranker, and that the reranker arm's ranked lists moved: an arm whose lists never moved is flagged inert, and so is a reranker that hands back its candidates in retrieval order on every query, with no reranker-free arm needed to compare against (on fewer than ten queries it says there were too few to tell). Every listed built-in implements its stage's interface, so any of them is a like-for-like control: ```python from lasagna.core.registry import registry [r["name"] for r in registry.list_rerankers() if r["implements_contract"]] # ['cross_encoder', 'combined', 'ensemble', 'mmr', 'colbert', 'llm_listwise', # 'monot5', 'llm_pointwise', 'flashrank', 'cohere'] ``` [The guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md#8-measure-it-on-a-benchmark) covers the 32 benchmarks, your own data, baseline arms (`closed_book`, `long_context`, `no_rag: true`), `--dry-run` with a cost estimate, the LLM response cache, and how to read, view and publish a result. ### Why the stages stay isolated A comparison is attributable only if the arms differ in the stage under test and nowhere else. Lasagna checks that rather than assuming it. - **A fixed interface per stage.** Components exchange only their stage's declared types, and function components get copies of what they are handed. A conformance suite checks that every registered component subclasses its stage's contract, does not mutate its input, and does not hand out chunks that share one metadata dict. From a source checkout (the tests are not in the wheel), run `pytest tests/test_abc_conformance.py tests/test_stage_isolation_behavioural.py`. - **A stage manifest per task.** Each run records what reached each of the eight stages: every setting, from the configuration the search actually resolved, and the component in the slot. - **A check across arms.** If two arms differ at a stage neither of them names, the run says so, the bundle is marked `UNDECLARED_STAGE_CHANGE`, and `lasagna results validate` refuses it, naming the stage and the settings that moved. An arm whose named change never reached its stage is flagged as inert, since its number is the control's under another name. ### Do two techniques compose, or do they overlap? The question two papers cannot answer between them. Hybrid search is published against a dense baseline; reranking is published against a baseline. Whether hybrid search still helps once a reranker is on does not follow from those two numbers: both may fix the same queries. Answering it needs all four cells measured on the same queries. Declare the 2×2 and the harness builds them: ```yaml # compose.yaml name: hybrid search with reranking benchmarks: - name: beir/scifact n_samples: 100 tracks: [retrieval] pipeline: base_profile: speed factorial: factor_a: enable_hybrid_search factor_b: enable_reranking ``` ```bash lasagna benchmark experiment compose.yaml lasagna results interaction "/results.json" --metric ndcg@10 ``` This one is keyless: `speed` embeds with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, BM25 needs no model, and reranking turned on uses the 92 MB MiniLM cross-encoder. A real run on 100 SciFact queries printed: ```text Cells 'reranking' and 'hybrid_search+reranking' returned identical ranked lists on all 100 shared queries. If the factor that separates them acts on retrieval, it did nothing in that cell, and the interaction below reflects that rather than an overlap between the techniques. expected if additive : -0.0081 actually observed : -0.0062 interaction : +0.0019 95% CI [-0.0318, +0.0355] p=0.9141 composition efficiency: not reported because the interaction is not significant (p=0.9141), so the ratio would describe noise additive (no detectable interaction) ``` On this corpus neither technique helped the dense baseline, and once the reranker was on, hybrid search changed none of the top ten. It was not skipped: it reordered the candidates, and that is all it could do here. Each cell asks for 40 chunks (ten documents, over-fetched four times), and `enable_hybrid_search` fuses the dense and BM25 lists by weighted rank, with `hybrid_alpha` 0.7 and `rrf_k` 60. A chunk only BM25 finds scores at most 0.3/60 = 0.0050, below the 40th dense chunk's 0.7/99 = 0.0071, so the fused 40 are the dense 40 in another order; on all 100 queries the reranker was handed the same 40 chunks in both cells. The cross-encoder scores each chunk on its own, so it returned the same top ten. For BM25 to bring in chunks of its own at this depth, `hybrid_alpha` must be below 0.62, or sweep the `hybrid_rrf` retriever, which fuses each list's top `hybrid_fusion_depth` (1,000) unweighted. The harness says so instead of reporting a 2×2 that only looks complete. The statistic is `(AB − neither) − (A − neither) − (B − neither)`, tested by sign-flipping each query's interaction contrast (all four cells of a query move together), with a t interval. Positive means the techniques compound; negative means they overlap. Factors are boolean settings, not component names: a component slot has no *off* level for the `neither` cell, and a factorial over anything else is refused before the first corpus is ingested. --- ## What's inside ### Pluggable RAG pipeline stages | Stage | Registered | Notes | |---|---:|---| | `retriever` | 5 | dense, BM25, SPLADE, hybrid RRF, hybrid convex (normalized score fusion) | | `reranker` | 10 | cross-encoder (any Hugging Face reranker, e.g. bge-reranker-v2-m3), ColBERT, monoT5, RankGPT listwise, LLM pointwise, FlashRank, Cohere Rerank, MMR, ensemble, combined | | `query_enhancer` | 8 | HyDE, Query2doc, step-back, Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, RAG-Fusion multi-query, expansion, least-to-most decomposition, combined | | `agentic_pipeline` | 7 | default graph (CRAG grading, Self-RAG-style gates, multi-hop planning), Self-Ask, IRCoT, FLARE, Adaptive-RAG, Self-RAG, legacy ReAct | | `generator` | 6 | concise, cited (ALCE), chain-of-thought, chain-of-note, closed-book, long-context | | `chunker` | 9 | fixed (characters, words or tokens), recursive, sentence window, Markdown header, semantic (Kamradt breakpoints), hierarchical, structure-aware, propositions (Dense X), contextual (Contextual Retrieval) | | `embedder` | 6 | any sentence-transformers model with its model card's prefixes, BGE-M3, OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, and the configured default | | `document_processor` | 4 | built-in (pypdf, pdfplumber, OCR), Docling, MarkItDown, PyMuPDF4LLM | `lasagna component list` prints them with each one's paper. Matryoshka truncation, late chunking, lost-in-the-middle reordering, context compression and speculative RAG are settings, and sweep the same way. ### Vector databases: six backends, one interface Milvus · pgvector · Qdrant · Weaviate · Pinecone · OpenSearch, behind one interface with a shared conformance suite asserting the same behavior against each. CI runs it on every pull request against Milvus Lite and Qdrant's local mode, which run in-process; the others need their service running ([details](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/vector_backends/README.md)). Each embedding model gets a vector collection of its own, so sessions on different profiles never mix vectors. ### RAG evaluation: 32 benchmarks, retrieval and generation metrics 32 benchmark entries over about 22 datasets (BEIR, RAGBench and KILT subsets count separately; `lasagna benchmark list` also shows `smoke`, a 24-document wiring check that is not counted, and any benchmark a plugin adds): BEIR (NFCorpus, FiQA, SciFact, ArguAna, HotpotQA), HotpotQA, SQuAD v2, MuSiQue, TriviaQA, Natural Questions, MS MARCO, FEVER, PopQA, Bamboogle, MultiHop-RAG, RAGBench, KILT, 2WikiMultihop. Your own JSONL, CSV or BEIR folder runs with no adapter ([own data](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/own-data.md)). `2wikimultihopqa` adds retrieval over the validation split's full contexts, including distractors, alongside the existing generation-only `wiki_multihop` entry. It reads the Apache-2.0 [official mirror](https://huggingface.co/datasets/xanhho/2WikiMultihopQA) at a fixed revision. Paragraph identity collapses whitespace and removes spacing around punctuation/symbols, preserving case and all non-whitespace characters. The exact rule first applies `" ".join(text.split())`, then `re.sub(r"\s*([^\w\s])\s*", r"\1", text)` before hashing. The first version of a title uses the title as its document ID; other versions add a stable hash of that normalized text. Formatting copies share one ID and the first original text is stored unchanged, giving 55,020 validation documents. `validation` is the default. `train` can be loaded as samples, but `load_corpus()` always supplies validation's corpus, so use `--split validation` for retrieval evaluation. | Family | Metrics | |---|---| | Retrieval | NDCG@k, precision@k, recall@k, F1@k, hit rate (success)@k, MAP, MRR, R-precision, complete (all-gold) recall@k for multi-hop questions | | Generation, no judge | exact match and token F1 (SQuAD-normalized; SQuAD v2 scored answerable and unanswerable separately), ROUGE-L, answer containment, answer similarity (embedding), abstention rate | | Generation, judged | faithfulness, context precision, context recall, factual correctness (RAGAS); citation recall and precision (ALCE) when answers cite; opt-in: answer relevancy, noise sensitivity, context relevance | | Operational | p50/p95/p99 latency (retrieval and generation, end to end), input and output tokens and LLM calls per query, with the judge's spend reported separately | Plus multi-objective tradeoff analysis, paired significance testing, and t confidence intervals. ### Interfaces and profiles Python SDK · REST API · MCP server · CLI · schema-driven configuration page. Five profiles: `default` (the settings file) and four presets, from `speed` (dense vector search only, keyless) through `standard` and `balanced` to `max_quality` (every retrieval feature on; the paper calls it Max-Reliable). `speed` turns off reranking, hybrid search, MMR, HyDE and the agentic loop. [Configuration](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#profiles) lists what each one runs and downloads. --- ## Install ```bash pip install lasagna-rag # core: ingest, embed, search, serve python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab # once: nltk's sentence tokenizer data ``` Lasagna supports Python 3.10 to 3.13. To reproduce a result exactly, install the versions the release was tested with. That constraints file was resolved on Python 3.12 and needs 3.12 or later (its numpy does not install on 3.10 or 3.11): ```bash pip install "lasagna-rag[eval]==0.1.0" -c https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dolev31/lasagna/v0.1.0/constraints/0.1.0.txt ``` `eval` adds the RAGAS metrics, benchmark loaders and statistics; the other extras (vector backends, document processors, LLM providers, the production stack) and the platform notes (CPU-only torch on Linux, Apple Silicon) are in [the guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md#2-install). `pip install lasagna` installs a different project; this one is `lasagna-rag`. Lasagna collects no usage telemetry, and turns off the usage events ragas would otherwise send (`RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=true`, unless you set it yourself). --- ## Model licenses Lasagna ships **no model weights**. They download from their upstream host on first use, each under its own license. Four selectable models are **not licensed for commercial use** (or state no license), including `naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil`, the default SPLADE sparse encoder, and `castorini/monot5-base-msmarco-10k`, the default monoT5 reranker; selecting one logs a warning naming the license. Before taking a configuration into a commercial product, read **[docs/model-licenses.md](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/model-licenses.md)**. ```python from lasagna.core.model_licenses import is_commercial_use_restricted is_commercial_use_restricted("naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil") # True ``` Benchmark corpora are never redistributed: they are fetched from their official sources and carry their own terms (`lasagna benchmark licenses`). --- ## Testing ```bash pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/live --ignore=tests/stress ``` Hermetic by default: no network, no external services, and the suite runs in a throwaway home directory, so it never touches your real `~/.lasagna` store. CI enforces it: sockets are blocked except loopback, and test order is shuffled on every run (pytest-randomly prints the seed). `tests/live/` needs a running stack; `tests/stress/` is long-running. Coverage is measured with branches on and floored in CI. --- ## Documentation **Start here: [Working with Lasagna](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md)**: install, write a component, compare it against a baseline, measure it on a benchmark, and publish the result. Every Python example in it is executed by the release gate on each run. | I want to... | Read | |---|---| | Measure a component, or run a sweep | [Guide](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/guide.md) | | Run on my own questions or documents | [Your own data](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/docs/own-data.md) | |
