licenses](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/src/lasagna/knowledge_evaluation_sdk/research/DATASETS.md) · [Citation](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/CITATION.cff) Each package directory has a short README for contributors, next to the code it describes. The guide, this README and `CONTRIBUTING.md` have their examples executed by the release gate; report anything elsewhere that does not work. --- ## The paper Lasagna is the framework behind **[Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)** ([Ido Levy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/idolevi31/), [Segev Shlomov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/segev-shlomov/), [Leshem Choshen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leshemchoshen/), 2026). The study tests 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora from 5K to 200K documents, and asks whether gains measured one component at a time survive when the components are combined.

| What the study found | Predicted | Realized | |---|---|---| | Retrieval gains do not add up: the three strongest single techniques, combined (NDCG@10) | +47% | +17% | | Faithfulness gains do carry over: one factor at a time versus the best full pipeline | +28% | +32% | **The best pipeline also changes with corpus size.** At 200K documents, the design that leads at small corpora trails by 13.7% NDCG@10, with the rank flip visible from 25K. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722) · [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29722) · [Project page](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/) · [Explainer video](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#explainer) · [Podcast (AI-generated, 25 min)](https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/#podcast) · [Pre-registration](https://github.com/dolev31/Lasagna-Retrieval-Augmented-Generation-Compositionality) ### Citing Lasagna If you publish work that uses Lasagna, please cite it: see [CITATION.cff](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/CITATION.cff), which GitHub renders as a ready-made BibTeX entry. To cite the paper: ```bibtex @misc{levy2026retrieval, title = {Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality}, author = {Levy, Ido and Shlomov, Segev and Choshen, Leshem}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2610.29722}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.CL}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722} } ``` If you also report a number from the evaluation harness, publish the results bundle with it: ```bash lasagna results bundle -o run.json ``` It carries the library versions, hardware, resolved sweep, corpus fingerprint and comparability key: what a reader needs to decide whether your number and theirs measure the same thing. `lasagna results validate` recomputes the key, the run id and every aggregate from its per-query scores, so a number edited after the run no longer matches its bundle. That is an integrity check against mistakes and naive edits, not a signature: anyone who edits a number can recompute the id, which is why the hub's trust model calls results self-reported. [hub/](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/tree/main/hub) has what is needed to run a public leaderboard for bundles: a generated JSON Schema, a pull-request validation workflow, and that trust model. --- ## License Apache 2.0: see [LICENSE](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/LICENSE) and [NOTICE](https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/NOTICE). Lasagna vendors no third-party source code.
sampled_files.pyproject.toml:
[project]
name = "lasagna-rag"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Composable RAG framework and evaluation harness: change one of eight pipeline stages, hold the rest fixed, and benchmark the change against a baseline."
readme = "README.md"
license = "Apache-2.0"
license-files = ["LICENSE", "NOTICE"]
authors = [
    { name = "Ido Levy" },
    { name = "Segev Shlomov" },
    { name = "Leshem Choshen" },
]
requires-python = ">=3.10, <3.14"
keywords = [
    "rag",
    "retrieval-augmented-generation",
    "retrieval",
    "information-retrieval",
    "llm",
    "vector-database",
    "reranking",
    "reranker",
    "hybrid-search",
    "evaluation",
    "benchmark",
    "mcp",
]
classifiers = [
    "Development Status :: 3 - Alpha",
    "Intended Audience :: Developers",
    "Intended Audience :: Science/Research",
    # No "License ::" classifier: PEP 639 supersedes it with the SPDX
    # `license` expression above, and setuptools rejects having both.
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.11",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.12",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13",
    "Topic :: Scientific/Engineering :: Artificial Intelligence",
    "Topic :: Text Processing :: Indexing",
    # The facets below are how PyPI's sidebar and /search/?c= browse work.
    # Without them the package is reachable by exact-name search only, which
    # is the one case where the searcher already knows it exists.
    "Topic :: Internet :: WWW/HTTP :: Indexing/Search",
    "Topic :: Software Development :: Libraries :: Python Modules",
    "Framework :: FastAPI",
    "Framework :: AsyncIO",
    "Environment :: Console",
    # NOT "OS Independent". The default vector store is milvus-lite, and
    # pymilvus gates that extra on `sys_platform != "win32"` -- so on Windows
    # `pip install lasagna-rag` reports success and the first upload dies with
    # pymilvus telling the user to install a package that will not install.
    # Windows needs WSL, or an external Milvus / another backend.
    "Operating System :: POSIX :: Linux",
    "Operating System :: MacOS :: MacOS X",
    "Typing :: Typed",
]

# Core: everything needed for `pip install lasagna-rag` followed by the
# README quickstart to work end to end — ingest a document locally, embed it,
# search it, serve it. Agent/browser-specific dependencies from the project
# Lasagna was extracted out of (playwright, browsergym, e2b, tavily, langfuse,
# langchain-ibm) are deliberately absent.
dependencies = [
    # Every core dependency is capped at its next major (for a 0.x release, at
    # 1.0): pymilvus 3, mcp 2 and a langchain-community minor each broke
    # installs that resolved the newest release. Extras are capped where a
    # break is known. constraints/ pins the exact set the release was tested
    # with.
    # LLM orchestration.
    # `langchain>=1.0` is a real floor, not caution: `agentic/agentic_rag.py`
    # imports `create_agent` from `langchain.agents` at module scope, which is a
    # 1.x API. Unbounded, a resolver was free to pick 0.3.x and break the import
    # of a core module.
    "langchain>=1.0,<2",
    "langchain-core>=0.3,<2",
    "langchain-openai>=0.2,<2",
    "langgraph<2",                        # agentic pipeline graph
    # Service surfaces
    "fastapi[standard]<1",
    "uvicorn<1",
    # Pinned below 2.0: mcp 2.0.0 removed `mcp.server.fastmcp`, which both
    # lasagna/mcp/server.py and sdk/integrations/mcp.py import. With an
    # unbounded range a fresh `pip install lasagna-rag` resolved to 2.0.0 and
    # the MCP server -- one of the four advertised interfaces -- failed at
    # import for every new user, while developers with an older resolved
    # version saw nothing wrong. Migrating to the 2.x API is tracked separately;
    # until then the bound is what makes installs work.
    "mcp[cli]>=1.23.0,<2",
    "fastmcp<4",
    "typer>=0.15.3,<1",
    # `lasagna init` is the first command in the README's shell quickstart and
    # imports this at 24 call sites. It was never declared, so that command
    # exited 1 on every fresh install with "pip install questionary". The e2e
    # docs phase only checks that `lasagna <cmd>` names a real command -- it
    # never runs bash blocks -- so nothing caught it.
    "questionary>=2.0,<3",
    # Imported directly by cli.py. It arrives transitively through typer today,
    # which means a typer release that drops it would break every CLI command
    # with no change on our side. Declared because we use it.
    "rich>=13.0,<16",
    # Configuration and runtime
    "dynaconf<4",
    "python-dotenv<2",
    "loguru<1",
    "pyyaml>=6.0.3,<7",
    "psutil>=7.0.0,<8",
    "httpx<1",
    # Default vector store (embedded; no server required)
    "pymilvus[milvus-lite]>=2.6.4,<4",
    # Embedding and reranking. Kept in core so the quickstart works on a bare
    # install; a slim client distribution for remote-backend-only use is
    # tracked as future work.
    "torch>=2.9.1,<3",
    "sentence-transformers>=5.1.2,<7",
    # monoT5 (a built-in reranker) ships its tokenizer only as a SentencePiece
    # model; without this package transformers cannot read it and
    # `reranker: monot5` failed on every install.
    "sentencepiece>=0.2.0,<1",
    # Document processing
    "pypdf>=4.0.0,<7",
    "python-docx>=1.2.0,<2",
    "pdfplumber>=0.11.9,<1",
    "beautifulsoup4>=4.14.3,<5",
    # `html2text` was here. It is GPL-3.0-or-later and was imported nowhere in
    # the package, so every install pulled a copyleft dependency into the user's
    # environment for no functional reason -- and a corporate legal review greps
    # the dependency tree, not the import graph.
    # Lexical retrieval for hybrid search
    "rank-bm25>=0.2.2,<1",
    # BM25 stems with nltk's Porter stemmer and the chunker splits sentences
    # with its punkt tokenizer. It was in two extras only, so hybrid search,
    # which core turns on, scored differently on a core install than on an
    # [eval] one, and every command printed two warnings about it. It is pure
    # Python. Its tokenizer data is a separate one-time download that nothing
    # here fetches for you: python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab
    "nltk>=3.9.1,<4",
    # Python 3.10 has no tomllib, and the built-in profiles are TOML: without a
    # parser they silently fall back to minimal defaults. It arrived only
    # through other packages.
    'tomli>=2.0,<3; python_version < "3.11"',
    # Imported directly; they arrived only through other packages before.
    "numpy>=1.24,<3",
    "pydantic>=2,<3",
    "pyjwt>=2.8,<3",  # REST session tokens (api/rest/session_token.py)
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
# Richer ingestion: semantic chunking and OCR for scanned documents
ingest = [
    "easyocr>=1.7.2",
    "pdf2image>=1.17.0",
]
# Structure-aware document conversion (tables, layout analysis)
docling = ["docling>=2.70.0"]
# Document to Markdown with Microsoft MarkItDown (the `markitdown` processor)
markitdown = ["markitdown[pdf,docx,pptx,xlsx]>=0.1.0"]
# PDF to Markdown (the `pymupdf4llm` processor). AGPL-3.0, so it is its own
# extra and deliberately not part of `all`.
pymupdf4llm = ["pymupdf4llm>=0.0.17"]
# BGE-M3 dense+sparse+ColBERT embedding
flag-embedding = ["FlagEmbedding>=1.3.0"]
# Entity-linked retrieval over a knowledge graph
graphrag = ["networkx>=3.0"]
# Evaluation harness: RAGAS metrics, benchmark loaders, statistics, plots
eval = [
    "ragas>=0.4.0,<0.5",
    # Not a lasagna import: ragas 0.4.3 (the newest release) imports
    # `langchain_community.chat_models.vertexai` at `import ragas`, and
    # langchain-community 0.4.2 removed that module. ragas declares the
    # dependency unbounded, so a fresh `[eval]` install resolved 0.4.2 and every
    # RAGAS score failed with "ragas is required ... pip install
    # lasagna-rag[eval]" while ragas was installed. 0.4.1 still ships the
    # module. Lift this once a ragas release stops importing it.
    "langchain-community<0.4.2",
    # ragas 0.4 needs datasets 4; saying so up front spares an older pip a
    # backtrack through every datasets 2.x and 3.x release.
    "datasets>=4.0,<6",
    "pandas>=2.0.0,<4",
    "scipy>=1.10,<2",
    "matplotlib>=3.7",
    "seaborn>=0.12",
    "jinja2>=3.0",
]
# Managed / self-hosted vector databases beyond the embedded default
vector-backends = [
    "pinecone>=5.0.0",
    "qdrant-client>=1.7.0",
    "weaviate-client>=4.4.0",
    # weaviate-client caps grpcio below 1.80, and the Google packages other
    # extras bring want the newest grpcio-status, which needs a newer grpcio.
    # An older pip installing extras one command at a time left the two
    # mismatched; bounding grpcio-status here keeps them a matching pair.
    "grpcio-status<1.80",
]
opensearch = ["opensearch-py>=2.4.0"]
# All three, per pgvector_backend.py:51-52 -- `psycopg[binary]` provides
# neither the `pgvector` adapter nor the connection pool, so the extra
# installed cleanly and left the backend silently unavailable.
pgvector = ["pgvector>=0.2.5", "psycopg[binary,pool]>=3.1"]
# Document storage backends
storage-s3 = ["boto3>=1.28"]
storage-all = [
    "boto3>=1.28",
    # datasets (in `eval`) caps fsspec, and s3fs pins fsspec to its own
    # release, so a newer s3fs and datasets cannot be installed together. The
    # bound keeps `storage-all` installable beside `eval` with any pip, in one
    # command or several.
    "fsspec>=2024.1,<2026.8",
    "s3fs>=2024.1,<2026.8",
    "gcsfs>=2024.1",
    "adlfs>=2024.1",
]
# Scheduled lifecycle jobs (document TTL, garbage collection). Background
# document processing with Celery is in `production`.
lifecycle = ["apscheduler>=3.10,<4"]
# What settings.lasagna_production.toml turns on: the Redis cache, quotas and
# rate limits, Celery background processing, Prometheus /metrics, OpenTelemetry
# tracing over OTLP, and the PostgreSQL database backend. Without these the
# production settings cannot run as configured.
production = [
    "redis[hiredis]>=5.0,<9",
    "celery>=5.3,<6",
    "prometheus-client>=0.20,<1",
    "opentelemetry-api>=1.24,<2",
    "opentelemetry-sdk>=1.24,<2",
    "opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc>=1.24,<2",
    "psycopg[binary,pool]>=3.1,<4",
]
# LLM providers beyond OpenAI (core), as listed in providers/llm_provider.py
providers = [
    "langchain-anthropic>=0.3,<2",
    "langchain-google-genai>=2.0,<5",
    "langchain-mistralai>=0.2,<2",
    "langchain-cohere>=0.4,<1",
    "langchain-nvidia-ai-endpoints>=0.3,<2",
]
# OCR engines beyond EasyOCR (in `ingest`). Tesseract also needs the
# `tesseract` program itself, from your system's package manager. The code uses
# the PaddleOCR 2.x API.
ocr = [
    "pytesseract>=0.3.10,<1",
    "paddleocr>=2.7,<3",
    "paddlepaddle>=2.6,<4",
]
# Web search fallback for corrective RAG (crag_web_search_fallback)
web = ["ddgs>=9,<10"]
# LlamaIndex components as pipeline stages (lasagna.from_llamaindex): the
# postprocessors, embeddings and retrievers you wrap are built with it. The
# adapter recognizes them by their methods and imports LlamaIndex only to build
# the nodes it hands a postprocessor. LangChain needs no extra: langchain-core
# is a core dependency.
llamaindex = ["llama-index-core>=0.12,<1"]
# Local LLM inference
local = [
    "langchain-huggingface>=0.1",
    "transformers>=4.40",
    "accelerate>=0.25",
    "langchain-ollama>=0.2",
]
# Everything
all = [
    "lasagna-rag[ingest,docling,flag-embedding,graphrag,eval,vector-backends,opensearch,pgvector,storage-all,lifecycle,production,providers,ocr,web,local]",
]

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/"
Repository = "https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna"
Issues = "https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/issues"
# PyPI renders these with their own sidebar icons. Documentation is the single
# highest-value link on that page: a visitor who arrived from search has no
# other signposted route to the guide.
Documentation = "https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/docs/"
Changelog = "https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md"
Paper = "https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722"

[project.scripts]
lasagna = "lasagna.cli:main"
# Point at server:main, not mcp.__main__ — that module calls main() at import
# time, so a console script targeting it would start the server twice.
lasagna-mcp = "lasagna.mcp.server:main"

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.3.5",
    "pytest-asyncio>=1.1.0",
    "pytest-cov>=5.0",
    # Same pin as CI and .pre-commit-config.yaml, so `ruff check .` agrees everywhere.
    "ruff==0.14.7",
    "pre-commit>=4.3.0",
    "detect-secrets>=1.5",
    "pip-audit>=2.7",
    "pip-licenses>=5.0",
    "requests>=2.32",
    # Used only by tests/stress. It was a CORE dependency and imported nowhere
    # in src/, so every install carried it to run tests the user does not have.
    "aiohttp>=3.9",
    # Checks the published hub schema against bundles we actually produce.
    # Available transitively today; declared so the test cannot start skipping
    # silently when a transitive dependency drops it.
    "jsonschema>=4.0",
    # Shuffles test order on every run (the seed is printed in the header), so
    # a test that passes only after another one fails in CI rather than
    # someday. Reproduce an order with -p randomly --randomly-seed=<seed>.
    "pytest-randomly>=3.15",
    # Lets CI run the suite with sockets blocked (--disable-socket), so a test
    # that reaches the network fails instead of passing online.
    "pytest-socket>=0.7",
    # Builds the PDFs the Docling processor tests feed it; without it those
    # tests skipped on every machine.
    "reportlab>=4.0",
    # Reads and validates the Colab notebook in examples/notebooks/, which is
    # the first thing many people run and is not otherwise executed by CI.
    "nbformat>=5.7",
    # Registers every metric with the real client (it is in `production`):
    # the no-op backend accepted a name with two label sets, Prometheus does not.
    "prometheus-client>=0.20,<1",
]
# The documentation site (mkdocs.yml). Exact versions: a theme or plugin minor
# release has changed markup and broken `mkdocs build --strict` with no commit
# here to point at. Build with `uv run --group docs mkdocs build --strict`.
docs = [
    "mkdocs==1.6.1",
    "mkdocs-material==9.7.7",
    "mkdocstrings==1.0.8",
    "mkdocstrings-python==2.0.10",
    "griffe==2.4.0",
    "pymdown-extensions==12.3",
    "mkdocs-autorefs==1.4.4",
    # Formats long signatures in the API reference; the same pin as the lint group.
    "ruff==0.14.7",
]

[build-system]
# 77.0 is the floor for PEP 639, which `[project] license = "Apache-2.0"`
# plus `license-files` above requires. On 68-76 the metadata fails
# validation; it built here only because the local setuptools is newer.
# `wheel` is vestigial for setuptools >= 70.
requires = ["setuptools>=77"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[tool.setuptools]
package-dir = { "" = "src" }

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
lasagna = [
    "py.typed",
    "settings.lasagna.toml",
    "settings.lasagna_production.toml",
    "**/*.jinja2",
    # Deployment manifests are shipped so `lasagna` users can run the stack
    "deploy/**/*",
    # Listed explicitly: setuptools' globs do not match dot-files, so the
    # template every deployment starts from was declared and silently absent
    # from the wheel. Found by the E2E install phase, which compares the built
    # wheel against the package-data patterns rather than trusting them.
    "deploy/.env.example",
    # Configuration UI: the prebuilt frontend bundle, produced by CI at release
    "configurator/frontend/dist/**/*",
    # Example experiment configs and the reference docs that describe them.
    # Without these, `pip install lasagna-rag[eval]` leaves a researcher with no
    # config to copy and no metrics reference on disk, while the README tells
    # them to run `benchmark experiment quickstart.yaml` -- a file that only
    # exists in a git checkout.
    "knowledge_evaluation_sdk/research/**/*.yaml",
    "knowledge_evaluation_sdk/research/**/*.md",
    "knowledge_evaluation_sdk/docs/*.md",
    # Agent skills. These have to be in the wheel: `lasagna skills install`
    # copies them out of the installed package, so a user who pip-installed
    # rather than cloned would otherwise get an empty list.
    "skills/*/SKILL.md",
]

[tool.setuptools.exclude-package-data]
# An operator's Kubernetes secrets (deploy/README.md, "Kubernetes"). The glob
# above matches the file system, not git, so a wheel or sdist built from a
# configured checkout carried them. `*` here spans directories.
lasagna = ["deploy/k8s/overlays/local/*"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
asyncio_mode = "auto"
markers = [
    "integration: requires external services (vector DB, API server)",
    "slow: long-running test",
    "needs_embedding_weights(*models): loads the named models (none named: the configured embedding model); skipped when Hugging Face offline mode is set and no cached copy exists",
]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["lasagna"]
branch = true
omit = [
    # Optional third-party agent adapters: exercised only when that framework
    # is installed, which it is not in CI by design.
    "*/lasagna/integrations/*",
]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
skip_covered = true
exclude_also = [
    "if TYPE_CHECKING:",
    "raise NotImplementedError",
    "if __name__ == .__main__.:",
    "@(abc\\.)?abstractmethod",
]
# Floor, not a target.
#
# Measured 2026-10-15 with the pytest line of scripts/ci-local.sh (sockets
# blocked, no external services, which is what CI sees): 51.3% combined
# (statement+branch, the `coverage report` TOTAL), 3,437 tests. It was 34% on
# 2026-08-19 while this floor stayed at 30. `branch = true` is on because this
# package's bugs have overwhelmingly lived in error branches, but the number
# gated below is the COMBINED total, not branch coverage alone: branch alone is
# materially lower, and the README badge used to name it while printing this
# figure.
#
# Set two points below the measurement to absorb ordering jitter and the
# Python-version matrix. This only ever ratchets UP. Lowering it to make a
# build pass defeats the point: if a change drops coverage, either it added
# untested code or deleted tested code, and both are worth a conversation.
fail_under = 49

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py310"
src = ["src", "tests"]

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
# A package's __init__.py imports names precisely so callers can reach them
# from the package root. Ruff cannot tell that from an unused import, and
# `__all__` is not consistently declared across this tree.
"__init__.py" = ["F401"]
"src/lasagna/**/__init__.py" = ["F401"]

# Type checking runs in CI (the lint job) on src/lasagna/sdk,
# src/lasagna/components.py and src/lasagna/core/base_components.py.
# Third-party packages are not installed for it, so their imports are Any.
[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.10"
mypy_path = "src"
explicit_package_bases = true
ignore_missing_imports = true
follow_imports = "silent"

# Modules in that target with errors at 0.1.0 (56 in total). Remove a module
# from this list once it checks clean; a new module is checked from the start.
[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = [
    "lasagna.components",
    "lasagna.sdk.client",
    "lasagna.sdk.config",
    "lasagna.sdk.exceptions",
    "lasagna.sdk.integrations.mcp",
    "lasagna.sdk.integrations.mcp_client",
    "lasagna.sdk.managers.citation_manager",
    "lasagna.sdk.managers.search_manager",
    "lasagna.sdk.remote_backend",
    "lasagna.sdk.types",
    "lasagna.sdk.utils.retry",
]
ignore_errors = true

# Awesome Agent Harness with stars > A curated list of tools, frameworks, and resources for **agent harness engineering** — the discipline of designing environments, constraints, and feedback loops that make AI coding agents reliable at scale. ## What is an Agent Harness? An agent harness is the infrastructure that wraps around an LLM coding agent. It's everything except the model itself: session management, context delivery, tool design, architectural enforcement, failure recovery, and human oversight. OpenAI's [Harness Engineering](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) blog defined the term: *"When a software engineering team's primary job is no longer to write code, but to design environments, specify intent, and build feedback loops that allow agents to do reliable work."* Their team built 1M+ lines of production code with zero human-written lines using this approach. Anthropic's Claude Code team [discovered the same principles](https://x.com/trq212/status/2027463795355095314) from the tool design side: the harness matters more than the model. Fewer, more expressive tools beat a long menu of narrow ones. Progressive disclosure — letting the agent recursively discover context across layers — outperforms loading everything upfront. *"Designing an agent's action space is as much an art as it is a science."* ## Core Principles From the two seminal references above: 1. **Humans steer, agents execute** — Engineers design environments and review outcomes, not write code 2. **Repository knowledge is the system of record** — If it's not in the repo, it doesn't exist to the agent. Slack threads, Google Docs, and tribal knowledge are invisible 3. **AGENTS.md is a table of contents, not an encyclopedia** — Point to deeper sources of truth; don't dump everything in one file 4. **Enforce architecture mechanically** — Custom linters, structural tests, and CI checks replace code review for invariants 5. **Agent legibility is the goal** — Optimize code for agent readability first, human readability second 6. **Fewer tools, more expressiveness** — Progressive disclosure and composable primitives beat sprawling toolkits 7. **See like an agent** — Read the model's outputs, watch where it struggles, and evolve the harness accordingly 8. **Corrections are cheap, waiting is expensive** — At high agent throughput, fix-forward beats blocking merge gates ## Contents * [What is an Agent Harness?](#what-is-an-agent-harness) * [Core Principles](#core-principles) * [Full Lifecycle Platforms](#full-lifecycle-platforms) * [Agent Orchestrators](#agent-orchestrators) * [Task Runners](#task-runners) * [Agent Harness Frameworks](#agent-harness-frameworks) * [Agent Runtimes](#agent-runtimes) * [Agent Knowledge & Memory](#agent-knowledge--memory) * [Coding Agents](#coding-agents) * [Requirements & Spec Tools](#requirements--spec-tools) * [Standards & Protocols](#standards--protocols) * [Methodologies & Workflows](#methodologies--workflows) * [Reference & Knowledge](#reference--knowledge) * [Contributing](#contributing) ## Full Lifecycle Platforms Tools that span from requirements to delivery with human-in-the-loop approval. * [Chorus](https://github.com/Chorus-AIDLC/Chorus) ⭐ 1,216 | 🐛 20 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-29 — Agent harness for requirements-to-delivery. Task DAGs, sub-agent orchestration (Agent Teams), proof of work, human approval gates. AI proposes, humans verify.

* [Paperclip](https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip) ⭐ 109,251 | 🐛 6,618 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source orchestration for zero-human companies. Budget/cost tracking, company templates (ClipMart), and autonomous agent coordination. Pushes the "agents execute" principle to its extreme — designed for fully autonomous operation with no human in the loop. * [Multica](https://github.com/multica-ai/multica) ⭐ 54,434 | 🐛 1,864 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source managed agents platform. "Turn coding agents into real teammates" — assign tasks, track progress, compound skills across sessions. Validates the core premise that agents need team-level management, not just individual harnesses. * [GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/automate-repository-tasks-with-github-agentic-workflows/) — GitHub Actions with coding agent engines (Copilot, Claude Code, Codex). Issue → agent → PR with sandboxing and permissions. * [Almirant](https://almirant.ai/?utm_source=awesome-agent-harness\&utm_medium=awesome-list\&utm_campaign=march-2026) — Operating system for human-agent teams. Persistent context across sessions, shared memory between agents, structured task lifecycle (plan → implement → review → deploy), and human approval gates. Designed for teams where humans and agents work together continuously — not just one-shot task execution. ## Agent Orchestrators Orchestrators solve the throughput problem: at high agent velocity, you need parallel execution with worktree isolation so agents don't step on each other. As OpenAI found, "corrections are cheap, waiting is expensive" — these tools maximize concurrent agent throughput. * [Everything Claude Code](https://github.com/affaan-m/everything-claude-code) ⭐ 293,783 | 🐛 190 | 🌐 JavaScript | 📅 2026-10-30 — Skills, instincts, memory, and security harness for Claude Code and Codex. * [Oh My OpenCode](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-opencode) ⭐ 70,535 | 🐛 2,024 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Performance optimization harness for OpenCode with 44 lifecycle hooks. * [Warp](https://github.com/warpdotdev/Warp) ⭐ 65,798 | 🐛 5,514 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-31 — Agentic development environment built for coding with multiple AI agents. * [Oh My Claude Code](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode) ⭐ 40,451 | 🐛 12 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Teams-first multi-agent orchestration for Claude Code. Ultrapilot mode runs 5 Claude Code instances in parallel Git worktrees, compressing 4-hour tasks to 50 minutes. * [Oh My Codex](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-codex) ⭐ 33,686 | 🐛 8 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Hooks, agent teams, and HUD for Codex. Adds lifecycle hooks and multi-agent coordination on top of OpenAI's CLI agent. * [Vibe Kanban](https://github.com/BloopAI/vibe-kanban) ⭐ 28,534 | 🐛 544 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-29 — Kanban-based orchestrator with git worktree isolation per agent. Supports 10+ coding agents. Enforces the "one agent, one worktree" pattern that keeps parallel execution clean. * [Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown) ⭐ 18,637 | 🐛 503 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-10-28 — Steve Yegge's multi-agent workspace manager. Docker-based with a "Mayor" orchestrator that distributes work as "beads" across agent "convoys." Includes web dashboard, git worktree isolation, and hook-based work state management. * [Trellis](https://github.com/mindfold-ai/trellis) ⭐ 15,071 | 🐛 89 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-09-29 — Git worktree-based multi-agent parallel harness. Isolates agents into separate worktrees for clean concurrent execution. * [Composio Agent Orchestrator](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator) ⭐ 13,952 | 🐛 845 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-10-31 — Agentic orchestrator for parallel coding agents. Plans tasks, spawns agents in isolated worktrees, autonomously handles CI fixes, merge conflicts, and code reviews. * [Emdash](https://github.com/generalaction/emdash) ⭐ 6,128 | 🐛 95 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-30 — Open-source Agentic Development Environment (YC W26). Runs parallel agents in isolated worktrees, locally or over SSH — making the "corrections are cheap" principle practical for remote teams. * [Scion](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/scion) ⭐ 2,071 | 🐛 80 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-10-31 — Google's open-source multi-agent orchestration testbed. Manages "deep agents" (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex) as isolated, concurrent processes — each gets its own container, git worktree, and credentials. Agent memory, chatrooms, and task management as orthogonal, pluggable modules. * [Octogent](https://github.com/hesamsheikh/octogent) ⭐ 1,418 | 🐛 23 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-04-20 — Claude Code multi-agent orchestration dashboard. Humans control worker agents directly from the orchestration layer with real-time visibility into parallel execution. * [Oh My AG](https://github.com/first-fluke/oh-my-ag) ⭐ 1,356 | 🐛 0 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Multi-agent harness for Google Antigravity with 6 specialized agents. * [Desplega Agent Swarm](https://github.com/desplega-ai/agent-swarm) ⭐ 977 | 🐛 28 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source multi-agent orchestration framework. Coordinates specialized AI agents (Claude Code-powered) through task delegation, session continuity, shared memory, and service discovery. Features include epics, scheduling, Slack integration, and cross-agent communication channels. * [ruflo](https://github.com/ruflo-ai/ruflo) — Claude agent orchestration with swarm mode. Coordinates multiple Claude Code agents for parallel task execution. ## Task Runners Task runners bridge the gap between issue trackers and coding agents. They embody the "humans steer, agents execute" principle: a human (or PM agent) creates the issue, the runner spawns an agent, and the output is a PR ready for review. * [Symphony](https://github.com/openai/symphony) ⭐ 27,879 | 🐛 0 | 🌐 Elixir | 📅 2026-09-15 — OpenAI's reference implementation of harness engineering. A daemon that polls Linear issues, spawns isolated Codex agents per task, and delivers PRs. Embodies "humans steer, agents execute" at scale. * [ralph](https://github.com/snarktank/ralph) ⭐ 22,099 | 🐛 75 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-02-02 — PRD-driven autonomous agent loop. Runs until all PRD items are completed, bridging spec-to-execution for single-agent workflows. * [Dexto](https://github.com/truffle-ai/dexto) ⭐ 659 | 🐛 88 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Coding agent and general agent harness for building agentic applications. * [Axon](https://github.com/axon-core/axon) ⭐ 350 | 🐛 167 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-10-31 — Kubernetes-native framework. Apply a Task CRD, get back a PR and cost in USD. TaskSpawner watches GitHub Issues. * [Linear Coding Agent Harness](https://github.com/coleam00/Linear-Coding-Agent-Harness) ⭐ 233 | 🐛 3 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-01-28 — Linear → autonomous coding agent → PR pipeline. * [Baton](https://github.com/shayne-snap/baton) ⭐ 10 | 🐛 6 | 🌐 Go | 📅 2026-03-07 — Go implementation of Symphony. Polls Linear for claimable issues, spawns isolated Codex workspaces per issue, streams workflow prompts, and cleans up on completion. * [GitHub Copilot Coding Agent](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/whats-new-with-github-copilot-coding-agent/) — Built-in GitHub issue → Copilot agent → PR. * [Claude World](https://claudeworld.ai/) — SaaS for leading Claude Code like a team director. Task-to-PR pipeline with built-in orchestration and monitoring. ## Agent Harness Frameworks Frameworks for building custom harnesses. Following the principle that "fewer tools, more expressiveness" beats sprawling toolkits, these provide composable primitives rather than opinionated workflows. * [DeerFlow 2.0](https://github.com/bytedance/deer-flow) ⭐ 84,760 | 🐛 989 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — ByteDance's open-source SuperAgent harness. Skill system with on-demand loading, sub-agent orchestration, sandboxed execution, and persistent memory. Built on LangGraph/LangChain. * [get-shit-done](https://github.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done) ⚠️ Archived — Meta-prompting and context engineering system for Claude Code. Structures work as milestone→phase→plan with progressive context delivery. * [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) ⭐ 30,829 | 🐛 234 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Agent harness built on LangChain/LangGraph. Implements progressive disclosure through planning tools and subagent spawning — agents discover context layer by layer rather than loading everything upfront. * [Compound Engineering Plugin](https://github.com/EveryInc/compound-engineering-plugin) ⭐ 25,793 | 🐛 98 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Cross-agent standardized plugin for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. Unified harness interface across multiple coding agents. * [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) ⭐ 14,412 | 🐛 853 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-30 — Microsoft's framework for building, orchestrating, and deploying AI agents and multi-agent workflows. Supports Python and .NET with structured orchestration patterns. * [GenericAgent](https://github.com/lsdefine/GenericAgent) ⭐ 14,376 | 🐛 202 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Self-evolving agent framework. Grows a skill tree from 3.3K lines of seed code, achieving 6x token efficiency reduction through learned capabilities. * [Hive](https://github.com/aden-hive/hive) ⭐ 11,131 | 🐛 1,093 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-26 — Outcome-driven agent framework. Queen agent generates agent graphs, harness manages state, checkpoints, and cost tracking. * [EvoMap Evolver](https://github.com/EvoMap/evolver) ⭐ 8,714 | 🐛 36 | 🌐 JavaScript | 📅 2026-10-30 — Genome Evolution Protocol (GEP) engine for agent self-evolution. Applies evolutionary algorithms to optimize agent behavior and harness configuration over time. * [Desloppify](https://github.com/peteromallet/desloppify) ⭐ 3,678 | 🐛 296 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-27 — Agent harness focused on making AI-generated code well-engineered. * [Zylos](https://github.com/zylos-ai/zylos-core) ⭐ 1,160 | 🐛 163 | 🌐 JavaScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Persistent agent harness for Claude Code. Tiered memory system, skill-based progressive disclosure, multi-channel communication bridge, task scheduler, and activity monitor — enabling autonomous, long-running agents that remember across sessions. * [Bridle](https://github.com/neiii/bridle) ⭐ 441 | 🐛 11 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-24 — TUI/CLI config manager for agent harnesses (Amp, Claude Code, OpenCode, Goose, Copilot CLI, Droid). * [Gambit](https://github.com/bolt-foundry/gambit) ⭐ 244 | 🐛 0 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-05-15 — Framework for building, running, and verifying LLM workflows. * [Harness Kit](https://github.com/deepklarity/harness-kit) ⭐ 103 | 🐛 1 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-07-15 — Patterns and engineering practices for building with AI agents. * [Meta-Harness](https://yoonholee.com/meta-harness/) — Academic approach to automated harness optimization using Claude Code for end-to-end harness tuning. ## Agent Runtimes The persistent infrastructure layer. Agent runtimes give coding agents long-running capabilities they lack natively: persistent memory, cron scheduling, multi-channel messaging, and sub-agent spawning. If orchestrators solve throughput and task runners solve issue-to-PR, runtimes solve "how does an agent stay alive and connected between tasks." * [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) ⭐ 393,532 | 🐛 7,894 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — AI agent runtime. Orchestrates agents across messaging channels with skill system, sub-agent spawning, and persistent session management. * [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) ⭐ 44,217 | 🐛 466 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Library for building stateful, multi-actor applications with LLMs. Functions as an agent runtime managing execution, state, and coordination of agentic workflows. Built on LangChain. * [Nanoclaw](https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw) ⭐ 31,061 | 🐛 1,035 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-30 — Lightweight alternative to OpenClaw that runs in containers. Connects to WhatsApp, Telegram, and other channels with a security-first, container-based isolation model. * [Claude Managed Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) — Anthropic's managed agent infrastructure. Pre-built, configurable agent harness running on managed infra — you define agent templates (tools, skills, repos), Anthropic provides the harness and execution environment. Decouples "brain" (Claude + harness) from "hands" (sandboxes + tools) and "session" (event log). Designed for long-horizon tasks as Claude's task horizon grows exponentially. ## Agent Knowledge & Memory Agents that run across sessions need persistent memory and shared knowledge. These tools solve the "context cliff" problem — without them, every new session starts from zero. * [claude-mem](https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem) ⭐ 107,246 | 🐛 151 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Automatic session capture with AI compression and injection into future sessions. Solves the stateless-agent problem by giving Claude Code persistent memory across runs. * [Hindsight](https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight) ⭐ 56,867 | 🐛 166 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Agent memory that learns. Automatically captures, indexes, and retrieves agent execution history to improve future task performance. * [CodeBurn](https://github.com/AgentSeal/codeburn) ⭐ 11,633 | 🐛 41 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Claude Code token usage analytics. Breaks down token consumption by task, enabling cost attribution and optimization. * [Honcho](https://github.com/plastic-labs/honcho) ⭐ 7,852 | 🐛 170 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Agent state memory library. Provides the persistence layer for stateful agents — session history, user context, and learned preferences. * [cq](https://github.com/nicholasgasior/cq) — Mozilla developer project enabling AI coding agents to share learned knowledge. A commons where agents deposit and retrieve solutions, avoiding redundant problem-solving. Has Claude Code and OpenCode plugins. ## Coding Agents The execution layer. In harness engineering, the agent is a commodity — the harness is the differentiator. These agents write code; everything above them determines whether that code is useful. * [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) ⭐ 259,075 | 🐛 52,211 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — Self-improving agent loop with persistent memory and self-generated skills. The agent that grows with you — learns from execution history and evolves its own capabilities over time. * [OpenCode](https://github.com/sst/opencode) ⭐ 223,481 | 🐛 3,764 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source coding agent with a plugin system (44 lifecycle hooks), server mode HTTP API, and TypeScript SDK. The most extensible harness integration point for custom workflows. * [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) ⭐ 132,416 | 🐛 25,811 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-31 — OpenAI's coding agent. Cloud and CLI modes. * [Pi Mono](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) ⭐ 119,139 | 🐛 315 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — AI agent toolkit: coding agent CLI, unified LLM API, TUI & web UI libraries, Slack bot, vLLM pods. Full-stack agent infrastructure in a single monorepo. * [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) ⭐ 108,645 | 🐛 766 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Google's CLI coding agent. * [Aider](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider) ⭐ 49,849 | 🐛 1,934 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-05-22 — AI pair programming in your terminal. * [GitHub Copilot CLI](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli) ⭐ 11,315 | 🐛 2,186 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-31 — GitHub's CLI coding agent. * [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/) — Anthropic's coding agent. The team's own harness pioneered "seeing like an agent" — progressive disclosure via skill files, fewer composable tools over many narrow ones. Agent Teams enables multi-agent coordination. The Claude Agent SDK extends the harness beyond coding. * [Kiro CLI](https://kiro.dev/) — AWS's CLI coding agent with spec-driven workflow. * [Amp](https://amp.dev/) — Sourcegraph's coding agent. * [Cursor](https://www.cursor.com/) — Anysphere's coding agent IDE. New Automations feature (March 2026) enables event-triggered agent launches from code changes, Slack messages, or timers. * [Warp AI](https://www.warp.dev/) — Terminal-native coding agent with built-in AI. Agentic workflows inside the terminal itself. ## Requirements & Spec Tools The planning layer addresses the biggest harness gap: agents can write code, but someone has to decide what to build. "Repository knowledge is the system of record" — these tools generate the specs and requirements that agents consume. * [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) ⭐ 144,199 | 🐛 221 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-10-30 — GitHub's spec generation toolkit. * [Archon](https://github.com/coleam00/Archon) ⭐ 23,794 | 🐛 171 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — First open-source harness builder. Makes AI coding deterministic and repeatable through structured harness configuration. * [Open Pencil](https://github.com/open-pencil/open-pencil) ⭐ 9,500 | 🐛 162 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source AI-native design editor (MIT). 75+ tools and an MCP server let coding agents read/write .fig files headlessly. * [Kiro IDE](https://kiro.dev/) — AWS's spec-driven development IDE. Generates structured specs and manages requirements. * [OpenSpec](https://github.com/FissionAI/openspec) — Spec-driven development CLI. Generate structured specs from natural language. * [agents.md](https://agents.md/) — Open standard for project-level agent instructions. Following the principle that "AGENTS.md is a table of contents, not an encyclopedia" — it should point to deeper sources of truth. * [Pencil](https://pencil.dev/) — MCP-enabled design canvas inside VSCode/Cursor. Design files live in the repo under Git version control, bridging visual spec to code generation. Closed source. * [Claude Design](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs) — Anthropic's design tool with direct handoff to Claude Code. Closes the design-to-code loop for solo developers and agent workflows. ## Standards & Protocols * [GitAgent](https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent) ⭐ 741 | 🐛 61 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-30 — Git-native, framework-agnostic standard for defining AI agents. Your repo is the agent: agent.yaml manifest + SOUL.md identity + RULES.md constraints. * [MCP (Model Context Protocol)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) — Open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. * [agents.md](https://agents.md/) — Open standard for project-level agent configuration. * [AGENTS.md](https://openai.com/index/introducing-agents-md/) — OpenAI's convention for repository-level agent instructions. * [ACP (Agent Communication Protocol)](https://agentcommunicationprotocol.dev/) — Open protocol for agent-to-agent and agent-to-harness communication. Enables interoperability across coding agents and orchestrators. * [HXA-Connect](https://github.com/coco-xyz/hxa-connect) — B2B messaging hub for AI agents. WebSocket-based real-time communication with org-scoped authentication, collaboration threads, @mention routing, and reply-to threading. Enables multi-agent coordination across different harnesses. ## Methodologies & Workflows Development methodologies and workflow definitions designed for agentic software development. * [AI-DLC Workflows](https://github.com/awslabs/aidlc-workflows) ⭐ 5,625 | 🐛 276 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — AWS's AI-Driven Development Life Cycle. A three-phase adaptive workflow (understand → plan → build) implemented as agent rules for Amazon Q, Claude Code, and other coding agents. Generates structured specs, enforces quality gates, and keeps humans in control. Based on the [AI-DLC methodology](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/ai-driven-development-life-cycle/). ## Reference & Knowledge ### Seminal References * [Harness Engineering: Leveraging Codex in an Agent-First World](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) — OpenAI's defining blog post. How they built 1M+ lines with zero human-written code. Introduced the concepts of repository knowledge as system of record, progressive context disclosure, and mechanical architecture enforcement. * [Lessons from Building Claude Code: Seeing Like an Agent](https://x.com/trq212/status/2027463795355095314) — Thariq (Claude Code lead) on designing agent action spaces. Fewer tools beat more tools. Progressive disclosure outperforms upfront loading. # Awesome Agent Harness with stars > A curated list of tools, frameworks, and resources for **agent harness engineering** — the discipline of designing environments, constraints, and feedback loops that make AI coding agents reliable at scale. ## What is an Agent Harness? An agent harness is the infrastructure that wraps around an LLM coding agent. It's everything except the model itself: session management, context delivery, tool design, architectural enforcement, failure recovery, and human oversight. OpenAI's [Harness Engineering](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) blog defined the term: *"When a software engineering team's primary job is no longer to write code, but to design environments, specify intent, and build feedback loops that allow agents to do reliable work."* Their team built 1M+ lines of production code with zero human-written lines using this approach. Anthropic's Claude Code team [discovered the same principles](https://x.com/trq212/status/2027463795355095314) from the tool design side: the harness matters more than the model. Fewer, more expressive tools beat a long menu of narrow ones. Progressive disclosure — letting the agent recursively discover context across layers — outperforms loading everything upfront. *"Designing an agent's action space is as much an art as it is a science."* ## Core Principles From the two seminal references above: 1. **Humans steer, agents execute** — Engineers design environments and review outcomes, not write code 2. **Repository knowledge is the system of record** — If it's not in the repo, it doesn't exist to the agent. Slack threads, Google Docs, and tribal knowledge are invisible 3. **AGENTS.md is a table of contents, not an encyclopedia** — Point to deeper sources of truth; don't dump everything in one file 4. **Enforce architecture mechanically** — Custom linters, structural tests, and CI checks replace code review for invariants 5. **Agent legibility is the goal** — Optimize code for agent readability first, human readability second 6. **Fewer tools, more expressiveness** — Progressive disclosure and composable primitives beat sprawling toolkits 7. **See like an agent** — Read the model's outputs, watch where it struggles, and evolve the harness accordingly 8. **Corrections are cheap, waiting is expensive** — At high agent throughput, fix-forward beats blocking merge gates ## Contents * [What is an Agent Harness?](#what-is-an-agent-harness) * [Core Principles](#core-principles) * [Full Lifecycle Platforms](#full-lifecycle-platforms) * [Agent Orchestrators](#agent-orchestrators) * [Task Runners](#task-runners) * [Agent Harness Frameworks](#agent-harness-frameworks) * [Agent Runtimes](#agent-runtimes) * [Agent Knowledge & Memory](#agent-knowledge--memory) * [Coding Agents](#coding-agents) * [Requirements & Spec Tools](#requirements--spec-tools) * [Standards & Protocols](#standards--protocols) * [Methodologies & Workflows](#methodologies--workflows) * [Reference & Knowledge](#reference--knowledge) * [Contributing](#contributing) ## Full Lifecycle Platforms Tools that span from requirements to delivery with human-in-the-loop approval. * [Chorus](https://github.com/Chorus-AIDLC/Chorus) ⭐ 1,216 | 🐛 20 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-29 — Agent harness for requirements-to-delivery. Agentic workflows inside the terminal itself. ## Requirements & Spec Tools The planning layer addresses the biggest harness gap: agents can write code, but someone has to decide what to build. Makes AI coding deterministic and repeatable through structured harness configuration. * [Open Pencil](https://github.com/open-pencil/open-pencil) ⭐ 9,500 | 🐛 162 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — Open-source AI-native design editor (MIT). 75+ tools and an MCP server let coding agents read/write .fig files headlessly. * [Kiro IDE](https://kiro.dev/) — AWS's spec-driven development IDE. Generates structured specs and manages requirements. * [OpenSpec](https://github.com/FissionAI/openspec) — Spec-driven development CLI. Generate structured specs from natural language. * [agents.md](https://agents.md/) — Open standard for project-level agent instructions. Following the principle that "AGENTS.md is a table of contents, not an encyclopedia" — it should point to deeper sources of truth. * [Pencil](https://pencil.dev/) — MCP-enabled design canvas inside VSCode/Cursor. Design files live in the repo under Git version control, bridging visual spec to code generation. Closed source. * [Claude Design](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs) — Anthropic's design tool with direct handoff to Claude Code. Closes the design-to-code loop for solo developers and agent workflows. ## Standards & Protocols * [GitAgent](https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent) ⭐ 741 | 🐛 61 | 🌐 Rust | 📅 2026-10-30 — Git-native, framework-agnostic standard for defining AI agents. Your repo is the agent: agent.yaml manifest + SOUL.md identity + RULES.md constraints. * [MCP (Model Context Protocol)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) — Open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. * [agents.md](https://agents.md/) — Open standard for project-level agent configuration. * [AGENTS.md](https://openai.com/index/introducing-agents-md/) — OpenAI's convention for repository-level agent instructions. * [ACP (Agent Communication Protocol)](https://agentcommunicationprotocol.dev/) — Open protocol for agent-to-agent and agent-to-harness communication. Enables interoperability across coding agents and orchestrators. * [HXA-Connect](https://github.com/coco-xyz/hxa-connect) — B2B messaging hub for AI agents. WebSocket-based real-time communication with org-scoped authentication, collaboration threads, @mention routing, and reply-to threading. Enables multi-agent coordination across different harnesses. ## Methodologies & Workflows Development methodologies and workflow definitions designed for agentic software development. * [AI-DLC Workflows](https://github.com/awslabs/aidlc-workflows) ⭐ 5,625 | 🐛 276 | 🌐 TypeScript | 📅 2026-10-31 — AWS's AI-Driven Development Life Cycle. A three-phase adaptive workflow (understand → plan → build) implemented as agent rules for Amazon Q, Claude Code, and other coding agents. Generates structured specs, enforces quality gates, and keeps humans in control. Based on the [AI-DLC methodology](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/ai-driven-development-life-cycle/). ## Reference & Knowledge ### Seminal References * [Harness Engineering: Leveraging Codex in an Agent-First World](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) — OpenAI's defining blog post. How they built 1M+ lines with zero human-written code. Introduced the concepts of repository knowledge as system of record, progressive context disclosure, and mechanical architecture enforcement. * [Lessons from Building Claude Code: Seeing Like an Agent](https://x.com/trq212/status/2027463795355095314) — Thariq (Claude Code lead) on designing agent action spaces. Fewer tools beat more tools. Progressive disclosure outperforms upfront loading. The harness must evolve with the model. * [Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic's guide: simple, composable patterns beat complex frameworks. ### Articles * [Building an AI-Native Engineering Team](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/build-ai-native-engineering-team/) — OpenAI's guide to structuring teams around AI-first workflows. * [The Emerging "Harness Engineering" Playbook](https://www.ignorance.ai/p/the-emerging-harness-engineering) — How OpenAI is retooling engineering teams. * [Conductors to Orchestrators: The Future of Agentic Coding](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/conductors-to-orchestrators-the-future-of-agentic-coding/) — O'Reilly overview of the orchestration landscape. * [My LLM Coding Workflow Going into 2026](https://medium.com/@addyosmani/my-llm-coding-workflow-going-into-2026-52fe1681325e) — Addy Osmani's specs-first approach. * [How the Claude Code Team Designs Agent Tools](https://www.anup.io/how-the-claude-code-team-designs-agent-tools/) — Analysis of progressive disclosure and tool subtraction in agent design. * [Your Agent Needs a Harness, Not a Framework](https://www.inngest.com/blog/your-agent-needs-a-harness-not-a-framework) — Inngest on why agents need runtime harnesses over frameworks. References OpenClaw and pi coding-agent patterns. * [Harness Engineering: Why Agent Context Isn't Enough](https://hugobowne.substack.com/p/harness-engineering-why-agent-context) — Hugo Bowne-Anderson on why the environment matters more than the model. * [Harness Engineering Is Cybernetics](https://x.com/odysseus0z/article/2030416758138634583) — George traces harness engineering back to Watt's governor and Wiener's cybernetics. The pattern repeats: sensor + actuator close the loop at a new layer. LLMs close it at the architectural layer — but only if you externalize your judgment into machine-readable specs. * [Agent Harness vs Agent Framework](https://x.com/tonykipkemboi/status/2031068470922670471) — Tony Kipkemboi (ex-CrewAI) maps agent development on a spectrum: raw API → framework (CrewAI/LangChain) → harness (OpenClaw). Frameworks give building blocks, harnesses give turnkey systems. * [The Anatomy of an Agent Harness](https://blog.langchain.com/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness/) — LangChain's Vivek Trivedy breaks down the harness into core components: state, tool execution, feedback loops, and enforceable constraints. Derives each piece from what models can't do out of the box. * [Harness Engineering](https://martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html) — Martin Fowler formally defines harness engineering as cybernetic governors for AI agents — feedforward guides and feedback sensors that form control loops around LLMs. The authoritative industry reference. * [Harness Engineering: Complete Guide 2026](https://www.nxcode.io/resources/news/what-is-harness-engineering-complete-guide-2026) — NxCode's comprehensive guide to harness engineering as a discipline: core concepts, agent=CPU/context=RAM/harness=OS analogy, and practical implementation patterns. * [The Harness as the Agentic Moat](https://businessengineer.ai/p/the-harness-as-the-agentic-moat) — Why the harness is the engineering response to model context loss, and why it constitutes a defensible competitive advantage. * [From Vibe Coding to Multi-Agent Orchestration](https://www.cio.com/article/4150165/from-vibe-coding-to-multi-agent-ai-orchestration-redefining-software-development.html) — CIO magazine on the shift from individual AI coding to orchestrated multi-agent development. Marks harness engineering's entry into mainstream business media. * [Harness Design for Long-Running Application Development](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps) — Anthropic's Prithvi Rajasekaran on building a three-agent (planner, generator, evaluator) harness for multi-hour autonomous coding sessions, with lessons on context resets, sprint contracts, and iterating harness complexity as models improve. * [Launching Claude Managed Agents](https://x.com/rlancemartin/status/2041927992986009773) — Lance Martin (Anthropic) introduces Claude Managed Agents: pre-built configurable harness on managed infra. Decouples brain/hands/session, designed for long-horizon tasks. Includes engineering blog, SDK docs, and usage patterns. * [The Design of Claude Managed Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) — Anthropic engineering deep-dive on building agents to scale with model intelligence as an infrastructure challenge, not just harness design. Agent config + environment template + stateful session as the three core primitives. * [Harness Engineering: Structured Workflows for AI-Assisted Development](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2026/04/07/harness-engineering-structured-workflows-ai-assisted-development) — Red Hat's take on harness engineering as a formal practice for enterprise AI development teams. * [Components of a Coding Agent](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/components-of-a-coding-agent) — Sebastian Raschka decomposes coding agents into model family + agent loop + runtime supports. Systematic breakdown of the harness stack. * [It's The Harness, Stupid](https://hyperdev.matsuoka.com/p/its-the-harness-stupid) — Developer benchmarks 8 coding agents across 5 challenges. Conclusion: choosing an AI coding tool is now an engineering decision, not a model selection decision. * [AI Agent Harness Pricing Split](https://thenewstack.io/ai-agent-harness-pricing-split/) — The New Stack reports on industry consensus: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft all agree the harness is the product — but diverge on pricing strategy. * [Skills Are Harness Engineering You Can Do in a Markdown File](https://www.ikangai.com/skills-are-harness-engineering-you-can-do-in-a-markdown-file) — Defining "Skills" as the most accessible form of harness engineering: structured Markdown files that shape agent behavior without code changes. * [Harness Engineering Guide](https://agentic-engineering.swmansion.com/becoming-productive/harness-engineering/) — Software Mansion's comprehensive guide to harness engineering as a practice. Covers environment design, constraint enforcement, and feedback loop construction. * [Multi-Agent Coordination Patterns](https://claude.com/blog/multi-agent-coordination-patterns) — Anthropic documents the "cheap executor + expensive advisor" pattern. Haiku for execution, Opus for decisions — reshaping the cost structure of agent orchestration. ### Talks * [The Future of Coding is Agents — Andrej Karpathy (YC)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fqVLjtvWgq8) — Landmark talk on the trajectory from assistants to agents. * [Agentic Coding — Armin Ronacher](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nfOVgz_omlU) — Creator of Flask on adopting agentic workflows in practice. * [12 Rules of Harness Engineering](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BabEnt6VjtE) — Practical rules derived from OpenAI's approach. ### Documentation Patterns * [harness-kit](https://github.com/deepklarity/harness-kit) ⭐ 103 | 🐛 1 | 🌐 Python | 📅 2026-07-15 — Engineering patterns for building with AI agents. * [agent-harness](https://github.com/MattMagg/agent-harness) ⭐ 12 | 🐛 0 | 📅 2026-02-23 — Principles, checklists, and invariants for AI coding workflows. ## Contributing Contributions welcome! When suggesting additions, include: * A one-line description of what the tool does * Why it belongs in this list (which layer of the stack it addresses) * New entries should be appended to the end of their respective category, not inserted at the top *** > _Enhansomed by [enhansome](https://github.com/enhansome) on 2026-10-31._

repository.description: Open-source catalog of go-to-market tools and workflows, written as markdown files any agent can run. Includes a read-only MCP server.
repository.name: growth-engineer
repository.readme:
growth.engineer

**Go-to-market tools and workflows, written as files any agent can run.** An open-source catalog of go-to-market companies, the functions an agent can call on each one, and workflows that chain those functions into a result. Every entry is a markdown file in this repository.

growth.engineer  ·  Connect your agent  ·  Contribute  ·  Develop

--- ## What is this? Handing a go-to-market tool to an agent means digging through docs written for people: which key to create, which endpoint to call, whether there is an MCP server, what a call costs. And a growth play that works usually lives in someone's notes, where no agent can run it. growth.engineer writes both down as markdown files an agent can follow: | Entry | Example key | What the file holds | | --- | --- | --- | | **Company** | `apollo` | Who the company is and how an agent reaches it: MCP server, CLI or API, and the credential each one needs. | | **Tool** | `apollo/enrich-person` | One function an agent can call: the exact MCP tool, CLI command or API endpoint, and the docs page that names it. | | **Workflow** | `funding-signal-outbound` | Up to ten steps across tools that reach a result: the one motion it serves, the outcome the user gets, the inputs to ask for, how to set up each tool, and the steps. | Paste a workflow file into Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any other agent and it can run the play. The file tells the agent to ask before it sends a message, spends money or changes data. Facts come from each vendor's own documentation, and every tool links the page that documents its call. --- ## Connect your agent The site runs an MCP server at `https://www.growth.engineer/mcp` (Streamable HTTP, no sign-in). Its `search` tool finds workflows, tools and companies, and `get` returns a file; neither changes anything. A third tool, `submit_feedback`, sends a bug report, request or question to the maintainers. Every workflow is also an MCP prompt that takes the workflow's inputs as arguments, and three more prompts (`contribute-workflow`, `contribute-tool`, `contribute-company`) walk an agent through adding to the catalog. | Client | How to add it | | --- | --- | | Claude | Settings → Connectors → Add → Add custom connector. Name it growth.engineer, paste the URL and click Add. | | Claude Code | `claude mcp add --transport http growth-engineer --scope user https://www.growth.engineer/mcp` | | ChatGPT | Plugins in the sidebar → Add → Create MCP App. Paste the URL, pick No authentication, accept the warning and click Create. | | Codex | `codex mcp add growth-engineer --url https://www.growth.engineer/mcp` | | Cursor | In `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, add `"growth-engineer": { "url": "https://www.growth.engineer/mcp" }` under `mcpServers`. | ### Or fetch the files Every file is public. There is no key and no sign-in. | URL | Returns | | --- | --- | | `/workflows/.md` | A workflow, ready to paste into an agent | | `/tools//.md` | One tool | | `/companies/.md` | A company and its tools | | `/tags//.md` | Everything with a tag, such as `/tags/capability/enrich-contacts.md` | | `/llms.txt` | The catalog's definitions and an index of every file | | `/llms-full.txt` | Every company, tool and workflow file in one document | | `/sitemap.xml` | Every page, with the date it last changed | A company, tool or workflow page also returns its file to a request with `Accept: text/markdown`. ```bash # A workflow file curl https://www.growth.engineer/workflows/funding-signal-outbound.md # The same file, by content negotiation curl -H 'Accept: text/markdown' https://www.growth.engineer/workflows/funding-signal-outbound ``` --- ## Contribute The catalog lives in this repository, and every addition or fix is a pull request. | To | Add or edit | Field reference | Agent skill | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Share a workflow | `workflows/.md` | [`workflows/README.md`](workflows/README.md) | [`add-workflow`](.agents/skills/add-workflow/SKILL.md) | | Add a company and its tools | `companies//company.md` and `tools/.md` | [`companies/README.md`](companies/README.md) | [`research-company`](.agents/skills/research-company/SKILL.md) | | Fix a fact | The file that states it | The same READMEs | | Check your work before you open the pull request. CI runs the same check. ```bash pnpm content:check # every problem in the catalog, each with its file ``` [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers the few rules worth knowing first. --- ## How it works There is no backend and no database. At build time, a compiler in `lib/content/` reads every file, validates it against a strict schema and resolves every reference. One renderer turns each company, tool and workflow into the file agents fetch, and Next.js prerenders every page from the same data. Deploying the site publishes the catalog. ``` companies/ workflows/ tags.yml │ ▼ lib/content/ read, validate, resolve, derive │ ▼ lib/catalog/render-markdown.ts one renderer, golden-tested │ ├─▶ pages, prerendered at build ├─▶ .md files, /llms.txt, /llms-full.txt └─▶ /mcp, the MCP server ``` The one runtime store is optional: an Upstash Redis that counts how often each workflow is copied, for its "Uses" and the Popular order. Without it, the counts are hidden. The footer's newsletter sign-up adds subscribers to Brew from a server action, with the Brew key kept on the server; without a key, it is hidden. Visits are measured with Vercel Web Analytics and Speed Insights, and AI crawlers and AI-referred visits with Notra. See [`docs/setup.md`](docs/setup.md#deploying-to-vercel). --- ## Project layout ``` growth-engineer/ ├─ companies// company.md and tools/.md (logos live on the CDN) ├─ workflows/.md one file per workflow ├─ tags.yml the tag vocabulary ├─ app/ Next.js routes: pages, .md files, /mcp, llms.txt, sitemap ├─ components/ layout, catalog lists, detail pages, UI primitives ├─ lib/ │ ├─ content/ the build-time compiler │ ├─ catalog/ keys, the markdown renderer, search, loaders │ ├─ mcp/ the MCP server's tools and prompts │ ├─ seo/ metadata, structured data, llms.txt │ └─ usage/ the optional copy counter ├─ tests/ Vitest: golden files, the content suite, schema checks ├─ docs/ architecture, data model, file format, setup └─ .agents/skills/ add-workflow, research-company ``` --- ## Local development **Prerequisites:** Node 22+ and pnpm 11 (`corepack enable` installs the pinned version). ```bash pnpm install pnpm dev # http://localhost:3000 ``` Edits to `companies/`, `workflows/` and `tags.yml` show on the next refresh. Add `.md` to a company, tool or workflow URL to see the file an agent gets. Nothing needs configuring. [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the optional variables: | Variable | Used for | | --- | --- | | `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` | The origin printed in `/llms.txt` and page metadata. On Vercel it defaults to the deployment's hostname. | | `KV_REST_API_URL`, `KV_REST_API_TOKEN`, `KV_REST_API_READ_ONLY_TOKEN` | The copy counter. Without them, the counts are hidden. | | `GITHUB_TOKEN` | The star count in the header. Without it, GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated requests an hour. | | `NOTRA_GEO_TOKEN` | AI-traffic analytics: the proxy reports AI crawlers and AI-referred visits to Notra. Without it, nothing is sent. | | `BREW_API_KEY`, `BREW_BRAND_ID`, `BREW_WELCOME_TRIGGER_ID` | The footer's newsletter sign-up, sent to Brew, and the trigger whose automation sends the welcome email. Without a key, the sign-up is hidden; without a trigger, no welcome is sent. | ### Scripts | Script | Does | | --- | --- | | `pnpm dev` | Starts the dev server | | `pnpm content:check` | Parses, validates and renders the whole catalog | | `pnpm check` | Biome and a fast typecheck | | `pnpm test:run` | The unit suite, including the content checks | | `pnpm tsc` / `pnpm lint` | The full typecheck and lint | | `pnpm build` | Production build | | `pnpm validate` | Lint, typecheck and tests together | | `pnpm hygiene` | Docs links, the content tree, unused code, duplicate dependencies | Heavy commands wait their turn behind a lock, so several worktrees can run checks without running out of memory. See [`docs/maintainers/validation.md`](docs/maintainers/validation.md). --- ## Deploy The site runs on Vercel with the settings in [`vercel.json`](vercel.json). Every page and file is generated at build time, so merging to `main` publishes the catalog. [`docs/setup.md`](docs/setup.md) has the details. --- ## Docs - [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md): the rules for changing the site, for people and coding agents - [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md): the request path and what prerenders - [`docs/data-model.md`](docs/data-model.md): what the build derives and every rule it enforces - [`docs/markdown-files.md`](docs/markdown-files.md): the format of a rendered file - [`docs/vision.md`](docs/vision.md): why the catalog exists and where it is going --- ## License [MIT](LICENSE) © Brew

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

# A new push to a pull request cancels its stale run. Pushes to main are keyed
# by SHA so every commit gets its own run: a concurrency group holds at most one
# pending run, so a shared main group would skip commits.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.ref || github.sha }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

# Least privilege: nothing here writes to the repository. Without this block
# the token inherits the organization default, often read-write, and every
# third-party action and install script would get a token that can push.
permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  NODE_OPTIONS: --max-old-space-size=6144
  # The heavy-command lock serializes local runs across worktrees; a CI runner
  # runs one job per machine, so the lock would only add latency.
  HEAVY_LOCK_DISABLE: '1'
  NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED: '1'

# `runs-on` reads the repository variables CI_RUNNER_SMALL and CI_RUNNER_LARGE
# (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), defaulting to ubuntu-latest.
# Moving to another runner fleet, or back after an incident, is then a settings
# change rather than a pull request that needs working CI to merge.

jobs:
  lint:
    # Biome: lint and formatting for the whole repository, in about a minute.
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - name: Lint and check formatting (Biome)
        run: pnpm lint

  typecheck:
    # `pnpm tsc` checks two TypeScript programs. Each is a matrix leg here, so
    # the job takes as long as the slower one and a failure names its program.
    name: typecheck (${{ matrix.program }})
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        program: [app, tests]
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      # scripts/typecheck.mjs owns the program list; the matrix passes a name
      # through, so adding a program is a one-line change there.
      - name: Type check
        run: pnpm tsc ${{ matrix.program }}

  build:
    # Builds the pull request, so a broken build or a client bundle regression
    # is caught before merge rather than by the deploy.
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_LARGE || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    # No env block: the catalog is built from the markdown tree, and every
    # variable in lib/env.ts is optional.
    timeout-minutes: 25
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Read the Next.js version
        id: next
        run: echo "version=$(node -p "require('next/package.json').version")" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      # Turbopack's persistent cache, keyed on the Next version and the
      # lockfile, with the commit SHA last: every run saves a fresh entry and
      # the next restores the closest one. An older cache is a valid warm start.
      - name: Restore .next/cache
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: .next/cache
          key: next-cache-${{ runner.os }}-${{ steps.next.outputs.version }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            next-cache-${{ runner.os }}-${{ steps.next.outputs.version }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-
            next-cache-${{ runner.os }}-${{ steps.next.outputs.version }}-

      - name: Build (Turbopack)
        run: pnpm build

      # Reads this build's manifests, so it runs in this job.
      - name: Client bundle budget
        run: pnpm perf:bundle

  test-unit:
    name: test (unit)
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      # No env block: the suite is hermetic. A test that needs a credential
      # should be fixed, not given a secret here.
      - name: Run unit tests (includes the content validation suite)
        run: pnpm test:run

  logos:
    # Every company's logo is on cdn.growth.engineer and whole: each `logo:`
    # URL answers with the bytes it names, and no logo file is left waiting in
    # a company folder. A contributor's new logo fails here until a maintainer
    # runs `pnpm logos:upload` on the branch (docs/maintainers/logos.md). It
    # reads the public CDN, so it needs no secret.
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - name: Every logo on the CDN
        run: pnpm logos:check

  test:
    # The one check to require in branch protection: it needs every other job.
    # `if: always()` makes a failed job turn this red instead of skipping it,
    # since branch protection treats a skipped required check as passing.
    if: always()
    needs: [lint, typecheck, build, test-unit, hygiene, logos]
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - name: Require every job
        env:
          NEEDS: ${{ toJSON(needs) }}
        run: |
          node -e '
            const needs = JSON.parse(process.env.NEEDS)
            const failed = Object.entries(needs)
              .filter(([, job]) => job.result !== "success")
              .map(([id]) => id)
            if (failed.length > 0) {
              console.error(`✗ required jobs did not pass: ${failed.join(", ")}`)
              process.exit(1)
            }
            console.log("✓ every required job passed")
          '

  hygiene:
    # Every gate runs even after one fails (`continue-on-error`), and the last
    # step fails the job if any did, so one run reports every problem.
    runs-on: ${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_SMALL || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Documentation links and AGENTS.md cap
        id: docs
        continue-on-error: true
        run: pnpm docs:check

      - name: Content tree (companies/, workflows/, tags.yml)
        id: content
        continue-on-error: true
        run: pnpm content:check

      - name: Unused files, exports and dependencies (knip)
        id: knip
        continue-on-error: true
        run: pnpm knip

      - name: Duplicate dependencies
        id: dedupe
        continue-on-error: true
        run: pnpm deps:dedupe:check

      - name: Require every hygiene gate
        env:
          OUTCOMES: ${{ toJSON(steps) }}
        run: |
          node -e '
            const steps = JSON.parse(process.env.OUTCOMES)
            const failed = Object.entries(steps)
              .filter(([, step]) => step.outcome === "failure")
              .map(([id]) => id)
            if (failed.length > 0) {
              console.error(`✗ hygiene gates failed: ${failed.join(", ")}`)
              process.exit(1)
            }
            console.log("✓ all hygiene gates passed")
          '
